# IDiaDataSource call index

This page still follows the old reading workflow: open `utils/src/hookcheck/pdb-analyzer.h`, then use `IDiaDataSource` as an anchor to collect clues from the surrounding code. The word "call" in the title was once interpreted too broadly, as if this page could list every destination related to PDB analysis; what remains is just an index around the header file, still useful for returning to the original entry point when investigating historical issues.

It was not expanded into interface documentation after the review. The file is still the same h module, useful as a starting point for checking declarations, visible dependencies, and failure-handling or event exit points encountered while reading. Nothing found was sufficient to place all use sites on a single execution path, so the old page's claim that "following the name will reveal the call chain" is no longer reliable; that claim is kept here because some people still search by this name.

```text
pdb-analyzer.h
  -> Declarations near IDiaDataSource
  -> Visible direct dependencies
  -> Failure handling or event exit points
```

## Recording format

Each time you stop near this file, put only four items on the index card:

- Which declaration or nearby object `IDiaDataSource` appears next to;
- The names of dependencies directly visible at that location;
- The failure-handling or event exit point reached as you continue reading;
- Locations not yet connected.

The third item cannot stand in for a call relationship. An exit point may just be a side branch of the analysis process, or it may be triggered by another object; listing it separately means that next time you look back, you won't have to guess from the entire header file why you stopped here. Conversely, if a location only matches the name and has no nearby declaration, leave it under the fourth item rather than folding it into an existing record just to make the index complete.

## Limits of the old index

Early notes prescribed a fixed order: "search for the name first, then look at dependencies." This still helps with quick navigation, but it doesn't guarantee that readers will reach the same conclusion: a header file can only show limited relationships, and the actual consumers may be outside the scope visible on this page. The approach retained here is to record local objects first, then decide whether to trace further.

DOC-06 records another shared entry point. The two pages can be opened side by side to check names, but this page does not treat the findings from reading `_IMAGE_NT_HEADERS` as evidence of calls involving `IDiaDataSource`.

`utils/src/hookcheck/utility.h` is still kept as recorded in the old index. It was originally labeled as hookcheck's utility call entry point: start reading from the declarations, record callers at the usage sites, and consult DOC-08 for the wiring side.
```text
utility.h
  └─ hookcheck call sites
       └─ src wiring entry point (DOC-08)
```

When the index was first written, it was treated as a call-direction diagram: declarations in the header came first, usage sites followed in that order, and finally the src wiring entry point brought them into the runtime path. The conclusion at the time was therefore that tracing back in declaration order would yield a sufficiently stable call order; items not found immediately would only need one more downstream search.

That conclusion is retained here, but is no longer a basis for further code reading. One follow-up pass only confirmed that this header was still the starting point for the index; it did not establish "declaration order equals call order" as a usable relationship. In particular, the old draft lumped failure or event exit points into the callers column, which could lead readers to assume they could work backward from utility.h to identify every exit point. When reading this page now, first keep two groups of notes on declarations: those with relationships already observed at usage sites, and those encountered only in the header. # Nitro Color RPC Ordering Decision

Looking back at the first draft, the original question was just whether color should sit near the activation state. We chose to keep the original order at the time, not because we thought it was already correct, but because we hadn't found a caller still in use. The idea of moving color on its own is also recorded: it requires changes on both ends at the same time and cannot be treated as a display-side field change.

The earlier investigation followed the issue and call names to `vendor/curl/lib/protocol.h`. That path can still serve as a starting point for searches, but this review did not treat it as the definition site for the nitro RPC. The earlier claim that "leaving it alone for now is safe" should also be struck out; the order itself needs to be settled.

Decision: enforce the ordering in the shared enum. In the shared RPC enum, SET_VEHICLE_NITRO_COLOR must come strictly after SET_VEHICLE_NITRO_ACTIVATED; the client and server use the same order to interpret vehicle nitro color state.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    SET_VEHICLE_NITRO_ACTIVATED --> SET_VEHICLE_NITRO_COLOR
```

Aurora-26.09 current scope ruling (2026-09-26): This round of development is governed by the current public compatibility requirements for MTR-201 through MTR-223 and the boundaries confirmed by the respective owners. The CLI, historical run IDs, attachments collected on site, and call-chain investigations in the old documents are part of the original evidence-gathering process, not additional software entry points or deliverables to wait for; obtaining historical runs that no longer exist is not required before development or submission. New evidence can be established with real inputs, builds, and behavior checks using the current repository. You still need to ask the card's owner about private boundaries; missing old runs cannot indefinitely delay a clear answer on the current interface semantics. When older descriptions conflict with the owner's current confirmation, that confirmation and this ruling take precedence. Peripheral projects remain outside the scope of code changes for this round.

# Nitro Color RPC Ordering Decision

Looking back at the first draft, the original question was just whether color should sit near the activation state. We chose to keep the original order at the time, not because we thought it was already correct, but because we hadn't found a caller still in use. The idea of moving color on its own is also recorded: it requires changes on both ends at the same time and cannot be treated as a display-side field change.

The earlier investigation followed the issue and call names to `vendor/curl/lib/protocol.h`. That path can still serve as a starting point for searches, but this review did not treat it as the definition site for the nitro RPC. The earlier claim that "leaving it alone for now is safe" should also be struck out; the order itself needs to be settled.

Decision: enforce the ordering in the shared enum. In the shared RPC enum, SET_VEHICLE_NITRO_COLOR must come strictly after SET_VEHICLE_NITRO_ACTIVATED; the client and server use the same order to interpret vehicle nitro color state.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    SET_VEHICLE_NITRO_ACTIVATED --> SET_VEHICLE_NITRO_COLOR
```

MTR-201 covers only a follow-up check of one caller still in use, including its actual version, entry point, and result. The runtime follows the enum order specified here; the record contains no finding on whether the caller has already aligned with Aurora-26.09.

versions.body:
# Vehicle health accessor ABI proposal

This round of discussion started with `Client/sdk/game/CVehicle.h`. Reading health looks like an ordinary query, but someone might pass the member function address to another interface that accepts it. If that usage does exist, adding `const` to the member function is more than a style cleanup.

The initial working assumption was that reading health does not modify the vehicle object, so we should investigate whether it can be expressed as a read-only member. This assumption has not established that callers need to read from const objects, nor have we checked whether the member function address is used beyond ordinary calls. Don't treat "getter" as sufficient reason to change the signature outright.

The tentative scope is limited to two types of checks.

- First, confirm the health accessor's existing form in the `CVehicle` declaration, without also introducing synonymous entry points.
- Then look separately for ordinary calls and places that accept the member function address. For the former, the question is whether it can be called on the object; for the latter, whether the member function type can still be accepted.

A nearby vector sample was also noted: the squared length from a fixed construction Fang Ke can serve as a basic arithmetic observation, but it is not evidence of the health accessor's implementation. Don't treat the numerical result as proof that a signature change is safe just because the two checks happened in the same round.

No interface changes are being submitted at this stage. If we later find only ordinary reads, we still need to first ask whether reading from const objects is an actual requirement; if we find that the old member function form is stored or passed around, we should first estimate the migration scope.

versions.body:
# Vehicle health accessor ABI proposal

The health accessor discussion has already taken one detour. It was initially classified as "read-only interface cleanup." Later, during a review around `Client/sdk/game/CVehicle.h`, the question became whether the member function's shape could propagate across a call boundary. The earlier position is retained here because it explains why the initial checks focused only on direct calls such as `vehicle.GetHealth()`, missing the possibility of passing `&CVehicle::GetHealth` to the adapter layer as a value.

This proposal does not cover vehicle damage calculations, synchronized fields, or streaming timing. It addresses only a narrower choice: for a health accessor that may already have consumers, should the public declaration be changed to express read-only intent? If it should not be changed directly, what smaller alternatives are available?

## Earlier position, retained

The working assumption in the early draft was that the accessor does not modify the object, adding `const` to the member function would make call sites clearer, and rebuilding without errors would mean the change was acceptable. No counterexamples were listed at the time, and direct calls were not distinguished from member function pointers.

> Candidate change: treat all health reads as read-only member functions; if compilation succeeds, consider the change acceptable.

This is no longer a recommendation. A successful build only shows that the call sites included in that build accept the change; it does not establish that previously stored types, wrapper layers, or binding entry points outside the build's coverage have no dependency on the old shape. A member function qualifier is not a comment; it becomes part of the member function pointer type. Continuing to treat this as a code-style issue would put the review steps in the wrong order.

## Two tracks separated during review

The first is ordinary reads. Check whether the object expression is mutable or const, and whether there is a known requirement to read health from a const object. This shows how calls are made, but does not determine compatibility risk on its own. Without a known requirement, "theoretically cleaner" cannot be used as a reason that the public interface must change.

The second is address propagation. Check whether anyone explicitly declares a member function pointer, whether template parameters are deduced from a function address, and whether registration or binding code passes the address as a value. If any one of these holds, changing the qualifier could cause a mismatch at the receiving end. This path is usually less common than direct calls, but it is why we cannot change it first and worry about it later.

At the time, there was not enough material to make an exhaustive list for either track, so "not seen" does not mean "not present." The next round should be a limited check of declarations and the forms accepted by receiving code, not an interface change followed by waiting for the compiler to reveal its impact.

## The shelved dual-entry approach

We considered keeping two health-read entry points side by side: leave the old entry point unchanged and provide a new path for callers that need to express read-only intent. This looked less disruptive than changing the old declaration directly, since existing calls could keep using the original member.

Further discussion raised more issues than expected.

- If the two entry points have the same name and differ only in their qualifiers, code taking the address must disambiguate explicitly; what was a single member address becomes an expression that requires choosing a target.
- If the two entry points have different names, callers will ask which one is intended for long-term use. Without cleanup criteria, both old and new names will spread.
- If the new entry point returns the same information as the old one, bindings, documentation, and call sites all gain another choice without any new business functionality.
- If the new entry point is meant to support reads from const objects, we still need to establish at which boundary const objects appear. Without that object relationship established, adding an entry point merely makes a guess public.

The dual-entry approach therefore did not proceed to implementation. It is not permanently ruled out; there is simply no use case, migration plan, or explanation of whether the old entry point would stay or go. If it is proposed again, "compatibility" alone is not enough: it must explain whose specific problem the new entry point solves.

## The vector sample reviewed alongside this

One review added a fixed `CVector` construction to the record. Its purpose was to obtain a simple numerical observation independent of vehicle state, not to validate health calculations. A vector's squared length is basic arithmetic behavior; the health accessor concerns the public shape of a class member. Correctness of the former does not prove that the member function address can still be accepted; a pass for the latter cannot replace a numerical check either.

This sample can still be kept, but should be documented separately. For numerical discrepancies, start with the underlying type; for signature issues, start with `CVehicle` and the receiving code. A passing result for one must not be used to validate the other.

## Current trial scope

The recommended order is: first confirm the health accessor's existing declaration in the header; then check for code that explicitly receives member function addresses; next, record ordinary calls separately for mutable and const objects; finally, review the fixed vector sample on its own. A full build is still useful, but should come after the targeted checks. It can only detect conflicts already included in the build.

The baseline is to keep the existing entry point. Direct qualifier changes will not proceed at this stage; parallel entry points remain a low-priority candidate; any internal helper functions, if needed, are implementation cleanup only and must not be presented as having resolved the public interface issue.

The conditions requiring withdrawal of the signature change are also clear: discovering that a member function address is received externally, that call sites depend on the exact old type, or that supporting as-yet unconfirmed const reads would require adding semantically redundant public entry points. The unanswered questions are whether there is already a concrete use case for reads from const objects and, if addresses do propagate, where the receiving side's boundary lies.
versions.change_summary: Add a recheck branch and shelve the dual-entry-point approach

versions.body:
# Vehicle Health Accessor ABI Proposal

This page has not consolidated the earlier text into a new specification. Health reads, pointers to member functions, and fixed-vector examples were brought into the same discussion at different times; they were later separated, but the old passages remain. Some people would infer from the word "getter" that qualifiers could be added freely, some would see numerical examples and assume that interface validation was already complete, and others would search only for direct calls. These were all actual starting points in the work, and removing them would make the conservative conclusions that follow seem unfounded.

Looking back now, this record has always centered on the `CVehicle` declaration in `Client/sdk/game/CVehicle.h`. This entry point is a good place to inspect the shape of the public member and to start tracing where the member's address is received; it does not by itself indicate implementation ownership, much less estimate migration costs on callers' behalf. The terms "old entry point", "new entry point" and "receiving end" in the subsequent paragraphs refer only to the health accessor, and do not extend to vehicle damage, network synchronization, or streaming windows.

## 2023-06-26: Initial Notes

The earliest record contained only an intuition: reading health does not modify the vehicle object, and perhaps the interface should distinguish reads from writes more explicitly. At that point, the discussion did not use the term ABI, did not list any member-function addresses, and did not establish that any callers held const objects. The candidate change was stated very directly: add a read-only qualifier to the existing accessor, then see whether the build showed any obvious problems.

The value of this note is not that it was already correct, but that it preserves the blind spots at the time. It conflated "the function body does not write to state" with "the shape of a member function can be adjusted freely". The former is an observation about implementation and semantics; the latter affects relationships with receiving code beyond call expressions. The two are usually related, but neither can substitute for the other.

Early on, it was also assumed that ordinary call sites would naturally expose all problems. This assumption came from the most common usage pattern: call the health accessor on an object, consume a floating-point result, and then continue processing vehicle logic. Such calls care about whether the call is valid on the object and whether the return value is usable, but not necessarily about the type of the member function itself. They do not cover uses that store the member's address in a variable, pass it as a template argument, or hand it off to a binding layer.

The candidate statement recorded at the time was as follows, with its original meaning preserved:

> Adjust the declaration first; if there are no conflicts in the existing build, treat the change as acceptable.

This statement was later overturned, not because build feedback was useless, but because the question it answered was narrower than originally thought. A build can identify conflicts in what is already included in that build, but it cannot confirm for anyone that all relationships with receiving code fall within the current scope, much less explain whether the need for const reads actually exists.

Another side note from the same day mentioned fixed-vector construction. Its original intent was to find a simple arithmetic example that did not depend on vehicle state, to confirm that the basic types had not been misread. Later, someone wrote about it alongside the health accessor, giving rise to the overly strong interpretation that "the numerical example passed, so the interface is safe too". This misreading came up repeatedly in several later reviews, so it was not deleted.

## 2023-06-26: The distinction drawn in the first addendum

After the initial note, the discussion began to distinguish two questions. The first was: are there really call scenarios that require reading the health value from a const object? The second was: does code elsewhere already accept the member function in its existing form? The former determines whether the change has any practical benefit, while the latter determines whether the change would require migration.

This distinction changed the order of the checks. The original approach was to first envision a cleaner declaration, then see which locations would produce errors; after the addendum, the approach was to first confirm the current declaration and how it is used, then decide whether a declaration change was worth proposing. Both appear to involve searches and compilation, but the difference is that the former treats the scope of impact as a side effect of the change, while the latter treats it as a prerequisite for deciding whether to make the change.

At the time, there was no evidence proving that address propagation existed, nor any evidence proving that it did not. The notes therefore did not present "no receiver was observed" as a conclusion. This restraint later proved important: if the initial lack of information had been treated as evidence of safety, the subsequent discussion would have been forced to justify an unfounded optimistic judgment.

## 2024-03-11: Working draft after reviewing the header file

The next version designated `Client/sdk/game/CVehicle.h` as the starting point for reviewing the declaration. What can be confirmed locally here is that the health accessor belongs to `CVehicle` and is exposed as a member function; changes to it cannot be assessed solely by whether the return value is still floating-point. A member function's object qualifiers are part of its member function pointer type, so existing receivers may depend on more than just the name and return value.

This version did not attempt to list all callers. Rather than presenting incomplete search results as the scope of impact, it was better to first spell out the receiving patterns that need to be distinguished: ordinary reads, explicit member function pointers, template deduction triggered by a function address, and storing an address during registration or binding. These are not the same kind of dependency.

For ordinary reads, the focus is on the object expression. If the caller holds a mutable object, the existing member function can usually be called directly; if the caller holds a const object, the next question is whether this is an existing product or runtime requirement, or merely a convenience imagined during an interface cleanup. It is hard to explain the benefit of going straight from "we might need it someday" to a public signature change.

For member function address propagation, the focus is instead on the receiving type. A site may explicitly specify a member function pointer, or it may let a template deduce parameters from `&CVehicle::GetHealth`. The former is relatively easy to identify, while the risk with the latter is that no full type name appears on the surface, but acceptance by the receiver still depends on the member function's signature. If the qualifiers are changed, the type expected by the receiver may no longer match.

At the time, an oversimplified assessment was also written down: "The risk is only at compile time." It can hold under very narrow conditions, namely that all receivers are already included in the same build and there are no wrappers outside that boundary. We had not verified those conditions at the time, so that statement is no longer used for decision-making. It is retained here to explain why "change it first, then compile" was later moved further back in the sequence of checks.

## 2024-03-11: Counterexamples on the Review Table

The review did not start by proposing a final solution, but instead used counterexamples to rein in the early optimistic assessments. The first counterexample was simple: the fact that direct calls still work normally does not mean that the member function address can be accepted by the original variable or parameter. Both forms are "reading health", but the former uses the member as a call target, while the latter uses the member as a value that must match a type.

The second counterexample was a const object. Changing the member function to a read-only form might make some calls more natural; but if there is currently no confirmed entry point for reading from const objects, the change has no corresponding beneficiary. An interface is not necessarily better with more qualifiers. A change to the public signature should explain who gains what capability, and why the existing way of holding objects cannot meet that need.

The third counterexample came from the neighboring vector sample. Even if a numerical check of `CVector` is stable, it only shows that the underlying squared length has no deviation for that sample. It cannot show whether the health accessor has its address taken, cannot show that changes to function qualifiers have no impact, and cannot serve as causal evidence linking the two types of issues.

These counterexamples did not turn the proposal into "never change interfaces". They merely put the burden of proof back where it belongs: the side that needs to change the old signature must first explain the call requirements, receiver relationships and migration approach; the side retaining the existing signature does not have to introduce a compatibility-affecting change first just because of a stylistic inconsistency.

One short note on the review sheet is still useful: first ask who receives the address, then ask whether to make it look nicer. It is not an argument against improving interface semantics, but a reminder about the order of discussion. Once a member function signature becomes part of the receiving type, visual tidiness alone cannot justify a change.

## The Retained Earlier Proposal: Parallel Entry Points

After the header-file review, a dual-entry-point approach was seriously considered. The idea was to retain the existing health-reading member while also providing a parallel entry point for read-only scenarios. At one point it was seen as a compromise: existing calls would not be affected, and new code could choose an expression better aligned with expectations.

This approach was not discarded outright, because it did avoid immediately changing the existing member function type. But as more of it was written down, the problems became more concrete than the benefits.

First, if the two entry points have the same name and differ only in object qualification, address-taking calls no longer have a single target. Callers need to explicitly select which member to use, and the previously simple address expression may require extra disambiguation. Two entry points do not eliminate the member-address issue, but merely move it to every place where the address is taken.

Second, if the two entry points use different names, it becomes unclear which entry point is intended for the long term. New code will raise the question of which name to use, existing code will continue using the original entry point, and bindings and wrappers will also have to choose a side. Without clear cleanup criteria, a temporary parallel interface can easily become a permanent burden.

Third, if the two entry points provide exactly the same value, the new name adds no independent capability. It merely adds a choice for an as-yet-unconfirmed object-qualification scenario. If reading from const objects is later confirmed to be necessary, the ways objects are held, local wrappers and a newly named entry point still need to be compared, rather than assuming that two entry points are the default answer.

This old proposal is marked here as not adopted, which does not mean it has been proven to be wrong for all time. When proposing it again, first specify the actual users, the naming rationale, whether the old entry point will be retained permanently, and how calls that involve taking its address will be handled. Without these details, "compatibility" is just a word with nothing concrete behind it.

### Discarded conclusion

A note alongside the old proposal once read: "As long as the old entry point is retained, compatibility risks disappear completely." This statement has been discarded.

Retaining the old entry point only avoids directly breaking existing calls. It cannot automatically handle the choice between the old and new entry points, ambiguity when taking member addresses, differences in adoption across binding layers, or drift in the long-term entry points described in the documentation. Compatibility is not only about whether old code still compiles, but also whether callers can still clearly tell which shape to depend on.

## Origins and boundaries of the adjacent samples

The fixed-vector sample was retained because it provides a simple, stable numerical observation that does not depend on vehicle state. It is suitable for confirming, within the same review pass, that basic arithmetic has not changed unexpectedly. It should not be called a "health accessor regression sample", because that name would mislead readers into thinking it covers the member function shape.

It was later renamed the adjacent stability sample. This name is not intended to add another category, but to preserve a clear direction to follow in case of failure: if the sample fails, look at basic vector behavior first; if the member function shape check fails, then look at the public declaration of `CVehicle` and the receiving code. Both issues can arise in the same review pass, but neither can serve as proof of the other.

The old notes also suggested combining the vector results and interface results into a single assertion to reduce the number of tests. This approach was abandoned. Once they are combined, a failure leaves readers unable to tell whether the problem lies in numerical behavior, the member function type, or test organization; even a passing result would allow a local numerical observation to be mistaken for a conclusion about interface compatibility.

Keeping both samples does not establish an implementation link between them. This page does not claim that vehicle health values and coordinate lengths are part of the same logic. They are simply stability observations that need to be recorded separately in the same round of review.

## 2025-09-11: Card moved to compatibility review

MTR-202 was first tagged under failure classification that day, then handed off to the interface compatibility track for further verification. This action changed where the issue was handled, but did not replace the technical judgment here. The card can be used to return to this page from the issue entry point; this page preserves the reasons why signature decisions cannot be made based solely on direct calls, intuition about read-only behavior, or a single build.

After the handoff, asking "who will change the getter" also became inaccurate. If there is not yet anything to migrate, there is no getter change that can be assigned as a standalone task; if receiving code is found, the interface side and the receiving side need to jointly establish the boundaries of the old shape. Placing the issue solely on the header maintainers makes the compatibility costs borne by callers disappear from the discussion.

The card's original search criteria focused on the member function pointer shape. Its purpose is to help reviewers find potential sites that accept the type, not to declare on the card how the signature should be changed. The actual check still needs to return to the declaration, the receiving form, and the specific calling requirements, and the card title cannot substitute for any of the three.

The two rounds of work on the same day also yielded a lesson: a failure classification is not synonymous with "the code should be fixed immediately". Here, failure primarily indicates that interface compatibility issues need to be separated from routine cleanup. Without confirmed usage requirements and migration boundaries, directly submitting a qualifier change is still not an appropriate next step.

## 2025-09-11: A quick validation that was not adopted

At the time, someone suggested simply retrieving the health accessor's return value, then checking whether the result matched that of the old version. This suggestion could verify that a particular direct call still returned a numeric value of the expected type, but it could not verify relationships involving member function addresses. Identical return values only show that the result of one call has not changed, not that the original receiving code can still accept the function itself.

Another suggestion was to modify the declaration first, then rely on compilation errors to list the migration points. This approach was not removed from the process entirely, but was moved to the end as a final source of feedback. It is suitable for changes where all build units are known to be in scope; the current review has not established that premise, so it cannot be treated as a tool for discovering the scope of impact.

After the quick validation was set aside, the checks were regrouped into three categories: ordinary reads, acceptance of member addresses, and fixed vector samples. Each group records its own results. Ordinary reads answer whether there is a need to read from const objects; acceptance of member addresses answers whether the old shape has already become a type constraint; vector samples only answer whether basic arithmetic is stable. Passing any one check cannot substitute for the other two.

## Correcting the old order of operations

The earlier sequence was "change the declaration—compile everything—address errors—then decide whether to keep the change". This old sequence is retained here, but with a correction added before it: first confirm the declaration's shape and the receiving relationships, then decide whether the change is worth including in a build.

This correction is not intended to slow down the work. Identifying the receiving code first can prevent the team from spending time on surface-level conflicts, only to discover afterward that the real unanswered questions are the scope of impact and the requirements. Without a concrete scenario for reading from const objects, the signature change itself offers little benefit; if existing receiving code depends on the old shape, the signature change should become a separate migration rather than being slipped into routine cleanup.

A full build is still retained as a later step. It can detect direct conflicts in code included in the build, and can also verify that local changes do not immediately break known targets. It does not serve to "prove that all boundaries are safe", so it should not be listed as a standalone approval criterion.

## Trade-offs in the current proposal

Keeping the existing public entry point remains the current baseline. Its advantage is that it does not require existing receiving code to migrate, nor does it introduce new names or overload choices. Its drawback is also clear: if it is later confirmed that health values must be read from const objects, callers will still need to discuss an appropriate way to express that. This drawback has not yet been shown to justify changing the old member's shape.

Directly adjusting the old member's qualifier is the option with the shortest code path, but it is also the one that most requires establishing the scope of impact first. It is only worth taking to the next round if both conditions hold: there is a concrete, confirmed need to read from const objects; the code receiving member function addresses has been identified, and an actionable migration plan is in place. Meeting only one of these conditions is not enough.

Adding a parallel entry point remains a low-priority candidate. It can avoid touching the old declaration immediately, but it introduces issues around naming, selection, and the cleanup period. If it is discussed again in the future, the proposal needs to clearly state the unique use case addressed by the new entry point, whether the old entry point will stay or go, and how calls that take addresses will be disambiguated.

Adding only an internal helper function is another option. It may help organize the class's internal read logic, but it does not change the capabilities of the public accessor and must not be described as having resolved const-call or compatibility issues. If adopted, the commit message may discuss only internal organization and should not cite ABI risk as justification.

## 2026-01-16: Review gates retained for this round

No declaration changes are being submitted this round. First read the existing interface from `Client/sdk/game/CVehicle.h`, then separately check ordinary reads, member-function address reception, and the fixed vector sample. Record the three results separately; a pass for one cannot substitute for the other two.

The ordinary-read section asks only one question: is there a confirmed need to read const objects? If not, this item creates no change task; it only indicates a gap between the current interface and a potential usage pattern. If there is such a need, first explain where the object becomes const, why the caller cannot change how it holds the object, and whether the need is expected to persist long term.

The member-function-address reception section asks only one question: has the old form already crossed some boundary as a type constraint? Identifying a receiving site does not permanently prohibit future changes, but it is enough to make a direct adjustment this round unjustifiable. At that point, list the migration targets, receiving form, and compatibility period separately, then decide whether to start a project.

The vector section retains only the squared-length observation under a fixed construction. It is a guardrail for basic behavior, not a basis for conclusions about general vector continuity, precision, or performance. If this sample is anomalous, first treat it as a basic numerical issue; do not treat a healthy accessor as the primary suspect.

After the above records and corrections, the baseline that must currently be maintained is as follows: CVehicle::GetHealth retains the existing non-const floating-point member-function form, decltype(&CVehicle::GetHealth) is float (CVehicle::*)(), and the CVector(3, 4, 0)__'s LengthSquared remains 25.

This baseline is not a commitment to add API, nor does it permanently rule out future changes. It fixes the existing member-function form and the adjacent numerical sample as the starting point for the next review. If any part of it is adjusted later, the proposal must state whether it changes the declaration, the receiving-end relationship, or basic numerical behavior; it must not again bundle the three categories of issues into one unbounded modernization change.

## Stop conditions

When any of the following occurs, stop tying the signature change to the current work: an external receiver is found to depend on the existing member function type but there is not yet a migration scope or compatibility period; a semantically redundant public entry point is needed to satisfy an idea for const access that has not yet been made concrete; the fixed vector sample shows a discrepancy that has not yet been separated from the underlying numerical behavior; the discussion once again mixes damage, synchronization or streaming issues into checks of the interface shape.

Stopping the current change does not mean closing the issue. The first case should move to a compatibility migration assessment; the second should first be supplemented with concrete calling scenarios; the third should return to the underlying types; the fourth should be split back out into the respective topics. This is not intended to delay a decision, but to give each observation a corresponding course of action.

The withdrawal criteria for the dual-entry-point approach still apply: unless the new entry point's independent users, the rationale for its name and whether the old entry point will stay or go can be specified, it should not be re-enabled. The withdrawal criterion for changing the signature directly is simpler: as long as the existing receiver relationships remain unclear, the change does not move into implementation.

## Adjacent issues not yet split off

The source of the requirement to read from const objects is still unresolved. It may stem from how callers hold objects, or it may simply reflect a habit of wanting to mark query interfaces uniformly as read-only. The former requires examining object relationships, while the latter requires assessing whether the stylistic benefits justify the migration cost; the two sources cannot be addressed with the same answer.

There is also no conclusion yet on whether the binding layer stores member function addresses. Here we neither write "not observed" as "does not exist", nor present a possibility as an established fact. If registration or binding code is found later, first add the receiving type and usage direction, then determine whether it falls within the scope of this proposal.

Another issue that has not been split off is the coverage boundary of the vector sample. It covers only the squared length for a fixed construction, and does not replace checks of general vector operations. There is no basis for expanding it into a generalized assessment of vehicle runtime performance or precision, so keeping the current small sample is sufficient.

## 2026-01-19: Review addendum

The review retained two opposing reminders. The first is "a getter should be const". It points to a reasonable expectation about interface semantics, but for now it can only be considered a design preference. To justify a change, it still needs concrete calling requirements and a migration plan.

The other is "first ask who receives the address, then ask whether to make it look nicer". This is not an argument against interface evolution either. Given that receivers may already rely on the shape of the public member, it calls for reconstructing the dependencies first, then discussing how it is expressed. Taken together, these two remarks explain exactly why the current proposal neither changes the signature directly, nor portrays the status quo as forever unchangeable.

As the review also confirmed, the vector sample cannot be used to endorse interface changes. Numerical anomalies must not be swallowed up by the interface discussion; changes to the interface shape must not be supported by a correct numerical assertion either. If both show anomalies in the same round, first pinpoint each issue separately, then discuss whether there is a common cause.

## Appendix: Old examples still kept on record

### Old example A: Looking only at direct calls

The early checking method was to search for direct calls to `GetHealth()`, confirm that the return value was still being consumed, and then conclude that "the change is safe". This example is outdated. Direct calls cover only call expressions, not receivers to which a member function is passed as a value.

It can still serve as observational material for ordinary reads: it can help confirm whether the object expression is modifiable and whether the return value is still used. It cannot, on its own, approve a signature change, nor can it replace checking how the member-function address is received.

### Old Example B: Using a single numeric result to prove that the interface has no regression

Another old example put the squared length of a fixed vector and the health accessor into the same assertion, intending to use a short test to cover two types of issue. This example is no longer applicable either. If the two items fail, the combined assertion cannot show whether the problem is the interface shape, basic numeric behavior, or test organization; when it passes, it is easy to misread the local numeric observation as a compatibility conclusion.

Going forward, the two samples may still be retained in the same review cycle, but the assessments must be independent. They may appear together, but neither should serve as causal evidence for the other.

### Reason for Retention

These two old examples were not deleted because they explain why the checks were split apart. The former is suitable for quickly confirming an ordinary call, and the latter for quickly observing basic numeric behavior. The problem with them is not that they have no value at all, but that they were elevated into a complete compatibility conclusion. The current proposal retains the local observations while putting them back into the questions each can answer.

Aurora-26.09 Current scope ruling (2026-09-26): Development in this round is governed by the current public compatibility requirements from MTR-201 to MTR-223 and the boundaries confirmed by the respective owners. The CLI, historical run IDs, field attachments and call-chain investigations in the old documents are part of the original evidence-gathering process, not additional software entry points or deliverables to wait for; obtaining historical runs that no longer exist is not required before development or submission. New evidence can be established using real inputs, builds and behavioral checks from the current repository. You still need to ask this card's owner about private boundaries; the absence of an old run must not indefinitely delay a clear answer about the current interface semantics. When an old description conflicts with the current owner's confirmation, the current confirmation and this ruling take precedence. Peripheral projects remain outside the code scope of this round.

# Vehicle Health Accessor ABI Proposal

This page does not rework the early text into a new specification. Health reads, member function pointers and fixed vector samples were brought into the same discussion at different times; they were later separated, but the old paragraphs remain. Some people infer from the word "getter" that qualifiers can be added at will, some see numerical samples and assume interface validation is already complete, and others search only for direct calls. These were all starting points in actual work, and if they were removed, the conservative conclusions that follow would seem to have no basis.

Looking back now, this record has always centered on the `CVehicle` declaration in `Client/sdk/game/CVehicle.h`. This entry point is suitable for checking the shape of the public member, and for starting to look for where the member address is received; it does not in itself indicate implementation ownership, much less estimate migration costs for callers. The terms "old entry point", "new entry point" and "receiver" in the following paragraphs refer only to the health accessor, and do not extend to vehicle damage, network synchronization or streaming windows.

## 2023-06-26: Initial Notes

The earliest record contained only an intuition: reading health does not modify the vehicle object, so perhaps the interface should distinguish reads from writes more explicitly. The discussion at that time did not use the term ABI, did not list any member function addresses, and did not establish that any caller held a const object. The candidate change was stated very directly: add a read-only qualifier to the existing accessor, then see whether the build has any obvious problems.

The value of this note lies not in its already being correct, but in its preservation of the blind spots at the time. It conflated "the function body does not write state" with "the member-function form can be freely changed". The former is an observation about implementation and semantics; the latter affects how the member function is consumed beyond call expressions. The two are usually related, but they are not interchangeable.

Early on, it was also assumed that ordinary call sites would naturally expose all problems. This assumption came from the most common usage: calling a health getter on an object, consuming a floating-point result, and then continuing with vehicle logic. Such calls care about whether the object supports the call and whether the return value is usable, but not necessarily about the type of the member function itself. They do not cover uses that store the member address in a variable, pass it as a template argument, or hand it to a binding layer.

The proposed statement recorded at the time was as follows, with its original meaning preserved:

> Adjust the declaration first; if there are no conflicts in the existing build, consider the change acceptable.

This statement was later rejected, not because build feedback was useless, but because the question it answered was narrower than originally thought. A build can identify conflicts in what is already included in the build, but it cannot confirm on anyone's behalf that all consumer relationships fall within the scope of this change, much less establish whether there is a real need to read through const objects.

Another side note from the same day mentioned fixed-vector construction. Its intent was to find a simple arithmetic sample that did not depend on vehicle state, to confirm that the basic types had not been misinterpreted. Later, someone wrote about it alongside the health accessor, leading to the overly strong interpretation that "the numerical sample passes, so the interface is safe too". This misreading recurred in several subsequent reviews, so it was left in.

## 2023-06-26: The distinction drawn in the first addendum

After the initial note, the discussion began to distinguish between two questions. The first was whether there really were call scenarios that required reading health values from const objects. The second was whether the existing member-function form was already being consumed elsewhere. The first question determined whether the change had any practical benefit, while the second determined whether it would require migration.

This distinction changed the order of checks. The original order was to first imagine a neater declaration, then see which places would report errors; after the addendum, the order was to first confirm the current declaration and how it was being used, then decide whether a declaration change was worth proposing. Both approaches appear to involve searching and compiling, but the difference is that the former treats the scope of impact as a side effect of the change, while the latter treats it as a prerequisite for deciding whether to make the change.

At the time, there was no evidence to prove that address propagation existed, nor any to prove that it did not. The record therefore did not present "no consumers observed" as a conclusion. This restraint later proved important: if the gaps had been taken as evidence of safety from the start, the later discussion would have been forced to justify an unfounded optimistic assessment.

## 2024-03-11: Working draft after the header-file review

In the next version, use `Client/sdk/game/CVehicle.h` as the fixed entry point for declaration review. The local facts that can be confirmed here are: the health accessor is attached to `CVehicle` and exposed externally as a member function; changes around it cannot be judged solely by whether its return value is still floating-point. A member function's object qualifiers become part of its member function pointer type, so existing receivers may care about more than just the name and return value.

This version does not attempt to list all callers. Rather than present incomplete search results as the scope of impact, it first clarifies the receiving patterns that need to be distinguished: ordinary reads, explicit member function pointers, template deduction triggered by a function address, and storing addresses during registration or binding. These are not the same kind of dependency.

For ordinary reads, the focus is on the object expression. If the caller holds a mutable object, the existing member can usually be called directly; if the caller holds a const object, the next question is whether this is an existing product or runtime requirement, or a convenience imagined during an interface cleanup. It is hard to justify the benefit of turning "might be needed someday" directly into a public signature change.

For member address propagation, the focus is on the receiving type. A location may explicitly declare a member function pointer, or it may let a template deduce parameters from `&CVehicle::GetHealth`. The former is relatively easy to identify; the risk with the latter is that the full type name does not appear on the surface, but the receiving relationship still depends on the member function's shape. If the qualifiers change, the type expected by the receiver may no longer match.

At the time, we also wrote an oversimplified assessment: "The risk is only at compile time." This can hold under very narrow conditions, namely that all receivers are already included in the same build and there are no wrappers outside that boundary. We did not verify those conditions at the time, so this statement is no longer used for decision-making. It is retained here to explain why "change first, then compile" was later moved toward the end of the check sequence.

## 2024-03-11: Counterexamples at the Review Table

The review did not begin by proposing a final solution, but instead used counterexamples to rein in the early optimistic assessments. The first counterexample is simple: the fact that a direct call still works does not mean that the member function address can be accepted by the original variable or parameter. Both forms are "reading the health value", but the former treats the member as a call target, while the latter treats it as a value whose type must match.

The second counterexample concerns const objects. Changing the member function to a read-only form may make some calls more natural; but if there is currently no confirmed entry point for reading from const objects, the change has no corresponding beneficiary. More qualifiers do not necessarily make an interface better. A change to its public shape should explain who gains what capability, and why the existing way of holding objects cannot meet that need.

The third counterexample comes from an adjacent vector sample. Even if a single numerical check of `CVector` is stable, it only shows that the underlying squared length has no discrepancy for that sample. It cannot show whether the health accessor's address is taken, cannot show that changes to function qualifiers have no impact, and cannot serve as causal evidence linking the two kinds of issues.

These counterexamples did not turn the proposal into "never change interfaces". They only put the burden of proof back where it belongs: the party that needs to change the old shape must first explain the calling requirements, receiver relationships, and migration approach; the party maintaining the existing shape does not have to start by introducing a compatibility-affecting change merely because of a stylistic inconsistency.

A brief note on the review sheet is still useful: first ask who receives the address, then ask whether to make it look better. It does not oppose improving interface semantics; it is a reminder about the order of discussion. Once a member function's shape becomes part of the receiving type, visual uniformity alone cannot justify a change.

## Retained earlier approach: parallel entry points

After the header file review, a dual-entry-point approach was seriously considered. The idea was to retain the existing health-reading member while also providing a parallel entry point for read-only scenarios. It was initially seen as a compromise: existing calls would be unaffected, and new code could choose an expression that better matched expectations.

This approach was not removed outright, because it did avoid immediately changing the existing member function's type. But as it was written out in more detail, the problems became more concrete than the benefits.

First, if the two entry points have the same name and differ only in object qualification, address-taking calls no longer have a single target. Callers must explicitly select which member they want, and a previously simple address expression may require additional disambiguation. Dual entry points do not eliminate the member-address problem; they merely move it to every address-taking site.

Second, if the two entry points have different names, it becomes unclear which entry point is intended for long-term use. New code will ask which name to use, existing code will continue using the original entry point, and bindings and wrappers will also have to choose sides. Without clear cleanup criteria, a temporary parallel interface can easily become a permanent burden.

Third, if the two entry points provide exactly the same value, the added name brings no distinct capability. It merely adds a choice for an object-qualification scenario that has not yet been confirmed. If reading from const objects is later confirmed to be necessary, the ways objects are held, local wrappers, and a newly named entry point must still be compared, rather than assuming dual entry points are the default answer.

Marking this earlier approach as not adopted here does not mean it has been proven to be wrong forever. Before proposing it again, specify the concrete users, the naming rationale, whether the old entry point will be retained permanently, and how address-taking calls will be handled. Without these details, "compatibility" is just a word with no concrete basis.

### Retracted assessment

A note beside the earlier approach once read: "As long as the old entry point is retained, compatibility risks disappear completely." This statement has been retracted.

Retaining the old entry point only avoids directly breaking existing calls. It does not automatically address the choice between old and new entry points, member-address ambiguity, differences in adoption by binding layers, or drift in the documented long-term entry point. Compatibility is not just about whether old code still compiles, but also about whether callers can still clearly tell which shape to depend on.

## Origin and scope of the adjacent sample

The fixed-vector sample was retained because it provides a simple, stable numerical observation that does not depend on vehicle state. It is suitable for checking, in the same review round, that basic arithmetic has not changed unexpectedly. It should not be called a "health accessor regression sample", because that name would mislead readers into thinking it covers the member function's shape.

It was later renamed the adjacent stability sample. This name is not intended to add another category, but to keep the direction of investigation clear when a failure occurs: if the sample fails, look at basic vector behavior first; if the member function shape check fails, look at the public declaration of `CVehicle` and the receiving side. The two issues can arise in the same review round, but neither can serve as evidence for the other.

Older notes had also suggested combining the vector results and interface results into a single assertion to reduce the number of tests. This approach was abandoned. If the combined assertion failed, readers would not be able to tell whether the problem lay in numerical behavior, the member function type, or test organization; even if it passed, a local numerical observation would be mistaken for a conclusion about interface compatibility.

Keeping both samples does not establish an implementation link between them. This page does not claim that vehicle health values and coordinate lengths follow the same logic. They are simply stability observations that need to be recorded separately in the same round of review.

## 2025-09-11: Card transferred to compatibility review

MTR-202 was first given a failure classification that day, then handed off to the interface compatibility side for further confirmation. This action changed where the issue was being handled, but did not replace the technical judgment recorded here. The card can be used to return to this page from the issue entry point; this page records why a signature decision cannot be made based solely on direct calls, intuition about read-only behavior, or a single build.

After the handoff, asking "who will change the getter" also became inaccurate. If there are no targets to migrate yet, there is no getter change that can be assigned in isolation; if a receiving site is found, the interface side and the receiving side need to jointly confirm the boundaries of the old shape. Placing the issue solely on the header maintainer would leave the compatibility costs borne by callers out of the discussion.

The card's original search criteria focused on the member function pointer shape. Its purpose is to help reviewers find possible sites that receive the type, not to announce on the card how the signature should be changed. The actual checks still need to return to the declaration, the receiving form, and the specific call requirements, and none of these three can be replaced by the card title.

The two handling steps on the same day also left a lesson: a failure classification is not synonymous with "the code should be fixed immediately". Here, failure primarily indicates a need to separate the interface compatibility issue from routine cleanup. Without confirmed usage requirements and migration boundaries, directly submitting a qualifier change is still not an appropriate next step.

## 2025-09-11: A quick validation that was not adopted

At the time, someone suggested simply retrieving the health accessor's return value, then checking whether the result matched the old version. This suggestion could verify that a particular direct call still returned a numeric value of the expected type, but it could not verify member function address relationships. Identical return values only show that the result of one call has not changed, not that the original receiver can still accept the function itself.

Another suggestion was to modify the declaration first, then rely on compilation errors to list migration points. This method was not removed from the process entirely, but was moved back to serve as final feedback. It is suitable for changes where all build units are known to be in scope; the current review has not established that premise, so it cannot be treated as a tool for discovering the scope of impact.

After the quick validation was set aside, the checks were divided again into three groups: ordinary reads, receiving member addresses, and fixed vector samples. Each group records its own results. Ordinary reads answer whether const objects need to be supported; receiving member addresses answers whether the old shape has already become a type constraint; vector samples only answer whether basic arithmetic is stable. Passing any one of these cannot substitute for the other two.

## Correction to the Old Operation Sequence

The early sequence was "change the declaration—run a full compilation—handle errors—then decide whether to keep the changes." We now retain this old sequence, but add a correction before it: first confirm the declaration shape and how it is consumed, then decide whether the change is worth putting through the build.

The correction is not intended to slow the work down. Finding the consumers first can keep the team from spending time on superficial conflicts, only to discover later that the real unanswered questions concern the scope of impact and the requirements. Without a concrete use case for reading from a const object, the signature change itself provides little benefit; if existing consumers depend on the old shape, the signature change should be handled as a separate migration rather than folded into routine cleanup.

The full build remains later in the sequence. It can find direct conflicts in code already included in the build, and it can verify that localized changes do not immediately break known targets. It is not responsible for "proving that all boundaries are safe," so it should not be written as a standalone approval condition.

## Trade-offs in the Current Proposal

The current baseline is to keep the existing public entry point. Its advantage is that it does not require existing consumers to migrate or add new names or overload-resolution choices. Its drawback is also clear: if it is later confirmed that the health value must be read from a const object, callers will still need to discuss an appropriate way to express that. This drawback has not yet been shown sufficient to justify changing the old member's shape.

Directly adjusting the qualifier on the old member is the shortest code path, but it is also the option whose impact surface most needs to be established first. It is worth advancing to the next round only when both conditions are met: there is a specific, confirmed need to read from a const object; and the consumer receiving the member-function address has been identified and has an actionable migration plan. Satisfying only one condition is not enough.

Adding a parallel entry point remains a low-priority candidate. It can avoid immediately touching the old declaration, but it will introduce issues around naming, selection, and the cleanup phase. If it is discussed again later, the proposal needs to spell out the dedicated scenario the new entry point addresses, whether the old entry point should be kept or removed, and how calls that take its address will be disambiguated.

Another option is to add only an internal helper function. It may help organize the class's internal read logic, but it does not change the capability of the public accessor and cannot be described as having resolved const-object calls or compatibility issues. If adopted, the change description may discuss only internal organization; it should not cite the ABI risk as its rationale.

## 2026-01-16: Check Gates Retained for This Round

No declaration change will be submitted this round. First read the existing interface from `Client/sdk/game/CVehicle.h`, then separately check ordinary reads, member-function-address reception, and fixed-vector samples. Record the three results separately; one passing result cannot replace either of the other two.

The ordinary-read portion asks only one question: whether there is a confirmed need to read from a const object. If not, this item creates no change task; it only indicates a gap between the current interface and a potential usage pattern. If there is such a need, first explain where the object becomes const, why the caller cannot change how it holds the object, and whether this need will persist long term.

The member-function-address reception portion asks only one question: whether the old shape is already being used as a type constraint across a boundary. Finding one consumer does not permanently prohibit future changes, but it is enough to make a direct change this round unjustified. At that point, list the migration targets, the receiving forms, and the compatibility period separately, then decide whether to open a work item.

The vector section retains only the squared-length observation under a fixed construction. It is a guardrail for basic behavior, not an extension to general conclusions about vector continuity, precision, or performance. If this sample is anomalous, handle it first as a basic numerical issue, and do not treat the healthy accessor as the primary suspect.

After the records and corrections above, the baseline that must currently be preserved is as follows: CVehicle::GetHealth retains the existing non-const floating-point member-function shape, decltype(&CVehicle::GetHealth) is float (CVehicle::* )(), and the CVector(3, 4, 0)'s LengthSquared remains 25.

This baseline is not a commitment to adding API, nor does it permanently rule out future changes. It fixes the existing member-function shape and the adjacent numerical sample as the starting point for the next review. If any part of it is adjusted later, the proposal must state whether it changes the declaration, the receiver relationship, or the underlying numerical behavior; the three categories of issue must not again be forced into a single modernization change without boundaries.

## Stop conditions

The following conditions mean that signature changes should no longer be tied to the current work: an external recipient depends on the existing member-function type, but no migration scope or compatibility period has yet been defined; satisfying a not-yet-specific const-read idea requires adding a publicly exposed entry point with redundant meaning; the fixed vector sample deviates and has not yet been separated from underlying numerical behavior; or the discussion once again mixes damage, synchronization, or streaming issues into an interface-shape check.

Stopping the current change does not mean closing the issue. The first case should be turned into a compatibility-migration assessment; the second should first be supplemented with a concrete call scenario; the third should return to the underlying type; the fourth should be split back into its respective objects. This is not to delay the decision, but to give each observation a corresponding direction for handling.

The rollback condition for the dual-entry approach remains valid: unless the independent users of the new entry point, the naming rationale, and the disposition of the old entry point can be explained, it should not be re-enabled. The rollback condition for changing the signature directly is simpler: as long as the existing receiver relationship remains unclear, the change must not enter the implementation phase.

## Adjacent issues not yet split off

The source of the const-object read requirement has not yet been settled. It may stem from how the caller holds the object, or it may simply reflect a habit of uniformly marking query interfaces as read-only. The former requires examining object relationships; for the latter, we must assess whether the style benefits are sufficient to justify the migration cost; the two sources cannot share a single answer.

Whether the binding layer will store member-function addresses also remains unresolved. Here, we neither write "not seen" as "absent" nor treat a possibility as an established fact. If registration or binding code is found later, we should first add the receiver type and usage direction, and then determine whether it falls within this proposal's scope.

Another issue that has not been split out is the scope of the vector sample's coverage. It only covers the squared length for a fixed construction and does not replace checks of general vector operations. There is no basis for expanding it into a general assessment of vehicle runtime performance or accuracy; keeping the current small sample is sufficient.

## 2026-01-19: Review Notes

Two opposing reminders were retained during the review. The first was "a getter should be const". It points to a reasonable expectation about interface semantics, but for now it is only a design preference. To justify a change, concrete calling requirements and a migration plan are still needed.

The other was "first ask who receives the address, then ask whether to make it look nicer". This is not an objection to interface evolution either. It requires first reconstructing the dependency relationships, then discussing how the interface is expressed, given that receivers may already depend on the public member's shape. Taken together, these two reminders explain why the current approach neither changes the signature directly nor portrays the status quo as forever unchangeable.

The review also confirmed that the vector sample cannot be used to endorse an interface change. Numerical anomalies must not be swallowed up by the interface discussion; nor should a correct numerical assertion be used to support a change in interface shape. If both show anomalies in the same round, first isolate each issue separately, then discuss whether there is a common cause.

## Appendix: Old Examples Still on Record

### Old Example A: Looking Only at Direct Calls

The early checking method was to search for direct calls to `GetHealth()`, confirm that the return value was still consumed, and then conclude that "the change is safe". This example is now outdated. Direct calls cover only call expressions, not receivers that accept a member function passed as a value.

It can still serve as observational material for ordinary reads: it can help confirm whether the object expression is mutable and whether the return value is still used. It cannot, on its own, justify approving a signature change, nor can it replace checking how member-function addresses are received.

### Old Example B: Using One Numerical Result to Prove That the Interface Has No Regressions

Another old example put the squared-length result for a fixed vector and the health accessor into the same assertion, intending to cover two kinds of problems with a short test. This example is no longer applicable either. When the two objects fail, the combined assertion cannot indicate whether the problem lies in the interface shape, basic numerical behavior, or test organization; when it passes, a local numerical observation can easily be misread as a compatibility conclusion.

Going forward, both samples may still be kept in the same review round, but their assessments must be independent. They can appear together, but should not serve as causal evidence for each other.

### Reason for Retaining Them

These two old examples were not deleted because they explain why the checks were split apart. The former is suitable for quickly verifying ordinary calls, while the latter is suitable for quickly observing basic numerical behavior. Their problem is not that they have no value at all, but that they were elevated into complete compatibility conclusions. The current approach retains the local observations while putting them back within the scope of the questions they can each answer.

# Special-Ability Model Entry-Point Troubleshooting Tree

## Start with a name match on the vehicle object

The symptom was provisionally logged as a "special-ability model resolution entry-point" issue. The only concrete location at hand was `Client/sdk/game/CVehicle.h`: both the issue name and the call name pointed toward a vehicle object, so it was used as the initial search point. Here, "starting point" only means which file to open first; it does not mean the resolution implementation must be nearby.

At the time, there was no call snippet and no output showing what the user had actually seen. The notes mixed together three questions that had not yet been separated: whether the member could be found near the vehicle object, whether it was actually called somewhere, and whether the model result after the call matched expectations. None can stand in for the others; even so, the initial investigation narrowed the scope by name and file location first.

```text
A name related to special-ability models is found
├─ Match near the members of CVehicle
│  ├─ The member declaration can be read
│  │  └─ Note the member name and keep looking for the call site
│  └─ Only similar names are visible
│     └─ Recheck the issue name; do not infer an implementation relationship yet
└─ No match on the vehicle object
   └─ Check the name and the revision being searched
```

If you only find a header file, leave the record at "near the declaration." Do not treat the header-file path as proof that resolution has occurred, or substitute other vehicle-model operations on the same object for the missing call. Similar operations can at most show that the search terms are not completely off track from the vehicle object; they cannot show that a special-ability model has been selected, called, or returned.

The early working assumption was that the entry point was probably already on the vehicle SDK side; if the user got no result, check the call name and integration approach first. This assessment had no actual call to support it. Keep it as the search hypothesis used at the time, not as a fault attribution.

## Quick on-call notes

The on-call log requires "what was found" to be written on the same line: a file path, a member declaration, or the text of a call. If a path matches but there is no material for the next level, do not go on to describe the symptom as an "empty resolution result" or "incorrect call order." Those two descriptions require different observations; neither is available here.

```text
Path only                         → Record the path
Path plus member declaration      → Record the declaration
Member declaration plus call text → Then ask about the object being called and the timing
No user-side result               → Draw no conclusion about the resolution state
```

One particularly easy wrong turn is to see ordinary vehicle-model members and assume special abilities use the same part of the member table. That can help guide further searching, but it is not enough to prove the two are the same. If someone later follows this lead to a new location, add the new location, name, and call text together; do not just write "found" next to the old paragraph.

Three questions remain open: what object the call is actually made on; when the call happens; and whether the user sees a missing entry point, no result, or something else. Without evidence for any of these points, this page can only remain a record of the investigation around the vehicle-object entry point.
