# Layered Timing Bucket Migration Decision

This page remains in the old category. It records not a set of migration rules that can be executed directly, but a judgment that once changed the direction of the investigation. The earliest record linked "Layered Timing Bucket Migration" to a file location; people who came later would follow that trail to search for `flag`, `acc`, and `prev`, then treat the similar names they found as parts of the same processing chain. This habit has already caused misinterpretations, but deleting the original text would prevent later reviewers from seeing where those misinterpretations began.

## The previously selected investigation target

The old record used `internal/mtasa-runtime`'s `v_prev` as background and `vendor/google-breakpad/src/third_party/linux/include/gflags/gflags_completions.h` as the investigation target. The wording here is not an ordinary index entry, but a decision that incorporates a judgment: first open that header file, then expand the investigation around similar names inside and outside the file.

There were three options at the time. The first was to treat the path as a direct entry point, with all subsequent searches continuing along similar names inside and outside the file. The second was to retain the path, then verify the reference relationships one by one. The third was to omit the filename and include only a problem description in the requirements history.

The first option was adopted because the earlier investigation had already reached this location through the issue name and call name. Continuing to use an existing target would allow the next search to begin immediately and give the discussion a concrete file, without having to start guessing again from the words "layered timing" every time. The weakness of this decision was not made clear at the time: a fixed file location can easily be read as implementation ownership, especially when the record does not also preserve the reference relationships.

For this reason, the original sentence in the first version, "This should be enough to indicate where time bucket migration is handled", must remain in the history. It was not a sentence added later to illustrate a counterexample, but a working judgment that was actually adopted at the time. The problem is not only that it was later shown to be too strong, but also that it conflated "we can start investigating here" with "this is where it is handled". These two propositions are not the same during an investigation.

## The narrower scope introduced by the case on the card

The later description in MTR-222 narrowed the target to a single CLI case in the current release and explicitly required preserving the parameter order and actual return status. The card first showed `design_compared`, then moved from To Do to In Progress. This change shows that the work moved from comparison to actual handling, but it did not automatically turn the old file path into evidence of parameter handling or return status.

There is a difference in levels here that the old record can easily obscure. The card describes what must be preserved in the external case; the old path describes where the early investigation began. Parameter order is part of the case requirements, and actual return status is also part of those requirements. Neither can be inferred directly from the filename `gflags_completions.h`, its directory, or the three search terms.

The three routes were compared again during review. Deleting the filename would be the easiest, but would remove the concrete origin of the old judgment; continuing to treat the filename as the migration entry point would be the most convenient, but would repeat the original misinterpretation of ownership; retaining the filename and downgrading it to navigation to neighboring code would allow a return to the original code neighborhood without presenting unconfirmed reference relationships as conclusions. The third route was the one actually adopted.

This choice did not turn the old judgment into a definite judgment to the contrary. It changed only how the file location is used in the record: the path indicates where the early investigation looked, while the references in `v_prev` provide the basis for checking the relationships. Whether there is runtime adjacency between the two cannot be confirmed from the old investigation text alone.

## How the file neighborhood is actually used

`vendor/google-breakpad/src/third_party/linux/include/gflags/gflags_completions.h` is in a third-party gflags-related directory. The available material provides only this frozen path, its revision, local declarations, and navigation to neighboring code. It does not provide an implementation chain connecting time bucket migration to this header file, nor does it identify the location of any specific declaration in the header corresponding to the CLI parameters.

Therefore, a review can still start with this file, but the act of starting must be separated from the ownership judgment. First return to the file neighborhood of `v_prev` and examine the same search clues as in the old record, `flag`, `acc`, and `prev`; then check whether references connect it to the runtime path. Merely finding the same file again shows only that the old entry point can be reproduced, not that the migration logic has been located.

The three terms do not carry equal weight here, either. They are matching terms left by the old investigation record, not a confirmed list of objects. `flag` can lead back to related naming, and `acc` and `prev` may also lead back to the same neighborhood; however, the existing record does not further explain whether each represents a time bucket, accumulated state, previous state, or merely appears in nearby declarations. Filling in the meanings of the terms as objects would once again turn search convenience into implementation fact.

There is also a historical reason for retaining the path. Deleting it entirely would lead later maintainers to think that the early investigation never relied on this third-party header file, and would remove the concrete reference point for "why the issue name and call name once pointed here". Retaining it does not mean continuing to endorse the original ownership judgment; it means that this path actually influenced the investigation order and deserves to remain in the history.

## The path cannot answer questions about the two external behaviors

MTR-222 requires preserving the parameter order and actual return status. The current page contains neither a parameter list nor return-status samples. What can be confirmed here is the requirement itself and the CLI case in which it applies, not how the parameters are ordered, where the status is produced, or which part of the references carries them.

The early record placed the "migration entry point" and "observed behavior" too close together, as though opening the path could answer both questions at once. From the second version onward, the decision was to separate them: the file path is used to revisit the old investigation; MTR-222 is used to check the case requirements for the current release. If the case requirements need to be traced into the code, the investigation should continue along the reference relationships of `v_prev`, rather than using the directory name as a substitute.

This also explains why "preserve the parameter order" cannot be rewritten as "no changes to the parameter definitions are needed", and why "preserve the actual return status" cannot be rewritten as "the current file already returns that status". The former adds a design conclusion that the material does not provide, while the latter adds an implementation location that the material does not provide. Both exceed what this decision record actually preserves.

## Branches remaining after review

If search efficiency is the only consideration, the first route remains attractive. It provides a specific file, and the old investigation record has already verified that this location can be reached through the issue name and call name. For anyone who needs to quickly reproduce the early line of thinking, this starting point is still valid.

If ownership risk is the only consideration, the third route is clean. It no longer makes the third-party header file imply a migration implementation, nor does it require the next person to first deal with a potentially misleading path. But it would erase a real historical choice and turn the later correction into an abstract warning with no recorded origin.

The second route preserves the respective uses of both sides. The path remains searchable as the old entry point, the reference relationships become the actual place for the next verification step, and the requirements card preserves the external case requirements. This decision did not create any new code objects, nor did it decide to replace parameters or return statuses; it merely split "where to investigate" and "what findings establish the relationship" into two steps.

In this record, the second step has not been filled in with concrete results. The material states only that the references in `v_prev` should be authoritative; it provides neither the members of the reference chain nor the locations of the parameter order and return status along that chain. The page therefore retains a narrow unresolved item, rather than filling in a complete mapping using filenames, search terms, or card titles.

## Relationship to the caller record

DOC-30 records the local work in Client · Caller Integration from the current entry point to the current revision. It can appear alongside this page because one preserves the old investigation entry point and the other preserves caller integration-debugging clues; it cannot draw conclusions about the case on behalf of MTR-222, nor can it turn the third-party header file into the owner of the caller.

When comparison is needed, first determine which level is being revisited. If the question is "why was this file opened in the early investigation", return to this page's path and search terms; if the question is "what must be preserved in the CLI case in the current release", consult MTR-222; if the question is "how did the caller reach the current revision", then consult DOC-30. The three intersect, but the records serve different purposes.

Treating DOC-30 as implementation proof here would introduce caller details that this page does not preserve; treating MTR-222 as proof of the path would work backward from external behavior to assert file ownership. The current material supports only side-by-side navigation and reading at separate levels, not combining them into an end-to-end chain.

## Excerpt from the old conclusion

> Layered Timing Bucket Migration is handled near the gflags completions header file, and all that is needed next is to search using `flag`, `acc`, and `prev`.

This passage is retained, but is no longer used as the current decision. It accurately reflects the convenience of the early choice, as well as what was omitted at the time: no reference relationships, no parameter order, no actual return status, and no verified chain connecting file adjacency to the CLI case. The original sentence is retained so readers can see how the old position took shape, not so they will continue making judgments on that basis.

The tone of "all that is needed next" in the old conclusion is also worth retaining. It shows that the search terms were considered a sufficient route forward at the time; the later review found that, at most, search terms could reproduce the old starting point, not replace reference verification. This difference is part of the page's own history and cannot be polished into an explanation that was never wrong.

## Scope of the decisions on the current page

Only three decisions remain. First, retain the old path so the early investigation can be traced. Second, treat that path as navigation to neighboring code, not as a confirmed location for handling the migration. Third, use MTR-222 to verify the parameter order and actual return status that must be preserved in the current release, without inferring their code locations from the path name.

These three decisions do not constitute a migration implementation plan. The page provides no modification steps, parameter ordering, return-value enumeration, or implementation operations for replacing files on that basis. This is not because the decision has been left blank, but because the current historical material has only corrected the entry-point judgment and has not yet preserved these finer-grained object relationships.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> OldEntry
    OldEntry: Old investigation entry point
    OldEntry --> RefCheck
    RefCheck: Reference relationship review
    RefCheck --> CliCheck
    CliCheck: Current CLI case verification
    CliCheck --> RelationUnknown
    RelationUnknown: Implementation relationship undetermined
```

In the diagram, "Old investigation entry point" corresponds to the search order once formed by the path, issue name, and call name; "Reference relationship review" corresponds to the verification performed after downgrading the path to navigation; "Current CLI case verification" corresponds to the release requirements in MTR-222. The final item remains undetermined, which does not mean that the migration does not exist, but that this page does not preserve the reference, parameter, and return-status mappings needed for confirmation.

Therefore, parameter order and actual return status remain the final unresolved objects on this page. The old path, issue name, call name, and three search terms are all insufficient to close this item. Following the path to revisit the early judgment remains valid; treating it as a confirmed migration boundary is no longer the approach used.

In this record, the second step has not been filled in with specific results. The material states only that the references in `v_prev` should be authoritative; it does not provide the members of the reference chain or the locations of parameter order and return status within that chain. The page therefore retains a narrowly scoped unresolved item rather than filling in a complete mapping with filenames, search terms, or card titles.

DOC-30 records local work in Client · Caller Integration from the current entry point to the current revision. It can appear alongside this page because one preserves the old investigation entry point and the other preserves clues for caller-side integration debugging; it cannot provide conclusions about the field case on behalf of MTR-222, nor can it turn the third-party header file into the caller's owner.

When comparison is needed, first determine which layer is being revisited. > The handling location for Layered Timing Bucket Migration is near the gflags completions header file, and subsequent searches only need to follow `flag`, `acc`, `prev`.

This passage is retained, but is no longer used as the current decision. It accurately reflects both the convenience of the early choice and what was omitted at the time: no reference relationships, no parameter order, no actual return status, and no verified chain linking the file's adjacency to the CLI field case. The original wording is retained so readers can see how the old interpretation took shape, not so they continue to base their judgments on it.

The tone of "subsequent searches only need to" in the old conclusion is also worth retaining. It shows that the search terms were considered a sufficient route for subsequent work at the time; later review found that the search terms could, at most, reproduce the old starting point, not replace confirmation of references. This distinction is part of the page's history itself and must not be polished into an account that was never wrong.

Only three decisions remain at present. First, retain the old path to make the early investigation traceable. Second, treat that path as navigation to adjacent code, not as a confirmed location for handling the migration. Third, use MTR-222 to check the parameter order and actual return status that must be preserved in the current release, without inferring their code locations from the path name.

These three decisions do not constitute a migration implementation plan. The page provides no steps for making changes, parameter ordering, return-value enumeration, or implementation actions that could be used as a basis for replacing files. Thus, parameter order and actual return status remain the last unresolved objects on this page. The old path, problem name, call name, and three search terms are all insufficient to close this item. title: Caller Integration Testing: Dual-State Incident Postmortem

versions.body:
# Postmortem: Dual-State Failure in Caller-Side Integration Testing

This incident involved the entry record for the same Client · Caller Integration object. At both visits, the entry labeled the displayed content as the current revision, but the revisions differed. The easiest misreading at the time was to assume that the object had switched twice or that two parallel states existed; the records available only establish that the entry made conflicting claims about which revision was current. They are not enough to conclude that the actual calls switched accordingly.

The affected area was the integration side's assessment of the call samples. Together, CEFLauncher.manifest and Main.cpp left behind a set of real call samples that could originally be used to compare against the adaptation boundary and integration feedback. After the entry state became inconsistent, the samples still existed, but they could no longer be directly interpreted under any one "current" revision. The integration target itself has its own schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria; this incident did not turn the entry discrepancy into a claim that those arrangements had changed.

## Incident Timeline

| Sequence | Situation recorded at the time | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Initial discovery | What the entry showed differed from the old record; initially, only the discrepancy was recorded, with no immediate judgment about which one was valid. | The old record was not overwritten. |
| Reviewing call samples | When reviewed against CEFLauncher.manifest and Main.cpp, the samples still showed where the calls occurred and the adaptation boundary the integration side needed to focus on. | The samples could not determine the entry's revision. |
| Returning to the entry | At the two time points, different revisions were each displayed as current. | The state conflict was recorded separately. |
| Incident closeout | The documentation version from the time was retained, and further retries stopped. | Pages obtained through repeated visits were not treated as new confirmation. |
| Follow-up consolidation | The original record, recovery page, and portions whose cause remained unknown were all retained. | Recovery actions and causal assessment were kept separate. |

The earliest working hypothesis leaned toward "the old record had not caught up." That explained the discrepancy seen the first time, but not why the entry later claimed to be current at both time points while giving a different revision at each. Whether the old record was lagging may still be part of the context, but it cannot be the sole basis for attribution. Accordingly, the path of "changing the old page to the new page" was not pursued further, and the call samples in Main.cpp were not treated as a state source.

## Impact on Call Samples

The roles of CEFLauncher.manifest and Main.cpp differed in this record. Together, they formed the actual call samples reviewed during integration testing; they can help someone taking over locate where the adaptation boundary lies and explain why the integration feedback was associated with the same object. They did not provide the reason why the revisions from the two entries differed.

On subsequent review, the first step is to keep three things separate: the revision displayed by the entry as current on a given visit, the call samples themselves, and the adaptation boundary referenced by the integration feedback. Treating the three as a single state would produce a conclusion that looks complete but cannot actually be verified. In particular, when the entry has been updated but the old record remains, the call samples may not have changed while the entry label has; conversely, an identical entry display cannot replace inspecting the samples.

This was also why retries were stopped at the time. Repeatedly reopening the entry could only produce another page display; it could not reconstruct the ordering of the two revisions, much less show which one the caller had adopted. The two states actually seen at the time were retained, rather than a transition path being filled in from the last page display.

## Recovery and Retention

The recovery page was retained to anchor the state records from that time to their respective time points; it does not mean that the root cause of the discrepancy has been found. The original record was also retained because the first mismatch with the old record was the starting point for the later judgment that a single page could not be the sole basis for review. With both materials retained, readers can see that the recovery action occurred while the cause remains unconfirmed, rather than mistaking recovery for completed attribution.

The integration target's schedule, maintenance assignment, and exit criteria remain as originally arranged. This record documents only the interruption to caller-side assessment caused by the inconsistent entry state; it does not record any resulting schedule adjustment, nor does it place the status of adjacent projects in the causal chain.

The current archive entry is `docs/adj-client/incidents/Client-caller-integration-same-object-has-two-states.md`. This location retains the version captured during the incident, so on review the entry discrepancy, call samples, and recovery record can be read along one timeline.

## Still Unconfirmed

- Why the entry produced a different current revision at each of the two time points.
- Whether the two revisions correspond to different display states of the same object, or whether the object's identification itself changed.
- Whether the entry-state changes have a direct relationship with the call samples seen in CEFLauncher.manifest and Main.cpp.
- Whether there were any unsaved intermediate states before or after retries stopped.

These questions are not answered in the incident materials. The recovery page addresses only the ability to compare the records again; it does not turn an unconfirmed cause into a definite conclusion.

versions.body:
# Caller Integration Testing Exit Window Checklist

During the exit window, check only three things: the exit action, the last visible result, and the exit action left on the adj-client side. This checklist does not determine whether the release succeeded; the responsible owner signs off separately. Once the window starts, do not turn the integration test session into a cleanup task, especially by cleaning up the test environment early just because you see asynchronous reclamation.

## Before the Window

1. [ ] Open `docs/adj-client/release/client-client-integration-exit-window-checklist.md` and find the `package number` for this run. If there is no package number, or the number cannot be matched to the integration test target you are looking at, stop here. Do not substitute a similarly named one.
2. [ ] Record the exit action to be checked in this window separately. The focus here is what the caller does when it finishes, not deciding whether integration is complete for the release.
3. [ ] Confirm that you can still obtain the last visible result. The result does not need to be interpreted as a pass or fail, but it must correspond to this exit window; if you cannot see it, do not proceed with further confirmation steps.

## During the Window

4. [ ] After initiating or verifying the exit action, first preserve the last visible result, then observe whether the test environment enters `asynchronous reclamation`. Seeing `asynchronous reclamation` only means that reclamation has started asynchronously; it is not a signal to clean up the environment.
5. [ ] Wait for the `streaming window` to appear. If it has not appeared, stop at this item. Do not mark the waiting state as complete or use it as a basis for adding a release conclusion.
6. [ ] Once the `streaming window` appears, put the exit action, the last visible result, and adj-client's exit action in the same handoff record. Include only what was observed during this window in the handoff record; leave unobserved items blank or explicitly state that they cannot be determined.

## Stop Conditions

Stop this window's checks if any of the following occurs: the `package number` is missing, the last visible result cannot be obtained, no `streaming window` is seen after exit, or only `asynchronous reclamation` is observed with no subsequent window. Stopping is not a reason to tear down the test environment. The recovery action has not yet been tried in the shared environment and cannot be treated as the default remedy here.

If another check is needed, start again from the package number in the checklist file and obtain the last visible result for this run again. Do not reuse the result left over from the previous window or fold release decisions not listed here into this checklist.

title: Caller Integration Path Proposal

versions.body:
# Caller Integration Testing: Route Proposal

Let's not rush to replace the existing integration as part of this comparison. We have two options: keep building on `offline loading`, or split out a separate `compatibility entry point`. I lean toward splitting out the entry point, not because the latter looks neater, but because the two paths exit at different points when they fail. Keeping them in the same caller path will mix together the behavior we observe later.

The advantage of `offline loading` is that it doesn't add another layer of entry-point selection logic, and existing callers don't have to change how they integrate right away. The problem is that it leaves compatibility handling in the original branch; when someone comes back from the streaming window, it's not yet clear whether they're seeing the loading path or the compatibility path. Splitting out the `compatibility entry point` would keep that decision logic separate, but it would add another integration choice and could make it look as though callers that relied on the old entry point are still supported.

I initially had the damage state down as the first thing to check after the split, but later realized that this was just a lead from memory. I haven't found a caller using it now, so I can't use it to prove that the two paths can already run independently. Don't write up the trial as already started.

Rollback hasn't been decided either. The conservative option is to restore only the old entry point; if the new entry point has already taken on some callers, restoring only the old one could leave two sets of decision logic in place. There isn't enough information here to decide which option is safer.

The material is in `docs/adj-client/proposals/not-adopted-Client-caller-integration-route.md` for now. When we pick this up next time, first establish which side the streaming window goes through, then decide whether a limited trial is worth doing.

versions.body:
# Caller Integration Test Route Proposal

This record was not turned into an integration guide. It records a caller-side integration-testing route for Client that was not adopted: why `offline loading` and `compatibility entry` were compared separately at the time, what concerns kept the trial from becoming an established plan, and how later actions on the cards changed the way the old material was reviewed. The judgments in the old paragraphs are retained under the conditions at the time; they cannot be treated as conclusions about current caller relationships.

The initial idea was simple. The existing path put offline processing and compatibility handling together. When a failure occurred, the caller could see only one exit, but it was difficult to tell whether that exit came from the loading process or whether compatibility checking had terminated early. The proposal was therefore to make the compatibility part a separate entry point. The purpose was not to redraw the client structure, but to give the two types of failure exits a chance to be seen separately.

There was no complete call chain available for verification at the time. The notes mentioned a streaming window and also mentioned that the damage state might be one of the current callers; the former only indicated that someone had seen mixed behavior at the window transition, while the latter was never supplemented with a verifiable usage point. Here, the inclination to "split the entry first" is retained, rather than being rewritten as a confirmed technical judgment.

## The two routes on the table at the time

**Continue with offline loading.**

The appeal of this route was that the scope of changes appeared small. The caller would continue entering through the existing entry point, while compatibility handling would simply continue to be filled in within the original branch. If the problem really occurred only during the offline stage, this choice would not force other integrating clients to reassess which side they belonged on.

But this premise had not been confirmed. The phenomenon near the streaming window showed that at least some observations could not naturally be explained as "pure offline loading." The original path kept entry selection, the loading process, and compatibility handling very close together; once an exit occurred, the record lacked clues that could separate them. Continuing to pile changes onto this area might mean fewer changes in the short term, but later make it harder to tell who depends on which behavior.

**Split out the compatibility entry.**

The split proposal was not meant to claim that the old entry was wrong, but to let the caller first indicate whether it was entering the compatibility branch or the original loading branch. The expected benefit was that the failure exits would no longer share the same decision logic: when an anomaly appeared later, it would at least be possible to first ask whether it occurred before or after entry selection, or in the loading process itself.

The cost was therefore also clear. Callers that previously did not need to select an entry explicitly would have to face a new integration boundary; in some places, if they merely continued using the old entry, the split could make it look as though they were still being treated as compatibility by default. More troublesome was rollback: if the new entry were simply removed after callers had already been distributed between the new and old entries, restoring the old entry would not amount to restoring the old behavior.

That was also why "split it out" was not written up as a decision at the time. The proposal was only a trial method for making failure locations easier to identify, not an already approved migration.

## Trial scope in the original plan

The old notes envisioned a very small comparison: one side kept `offline loading`, while the other went through the candidate `compatibility entry`. The point of the comparison was not to move all client paths over, but to see whether the same type of integration feedback would still be merged into one result on the two paths. If it yielded only one successful display, or merely changed the visible label without making the caller's entry selection distinguishable, that would not count as support for the split.

The "same type" was not written out as a complete list at the time. The damage state was noted alongside it because it might pass through the current caller; later, there was not enough material to confirm its actual location. The streaming window was also only an observation point to revisit and should not be miswritten as a completed trial sample. The old draft placed these terms side by side in a way that made them look like an existing experiment; in fact, it only intended to use them to find a contrasting input.

The anticipated stopping conditions were somewhat clearer than the starting conditions: if, after splitting the entry, it was still impossible to tell where the exit came from, or if connecting to the new entry required crossing the current interface, this trial method would be stopped. If the original streaming window could not be restored when exiting, it should not be left in a half-integrated state. Here, "restore" means only returning to the entry arrangement from before the split; it contains no commitment regarding the behavior of other clients.

## Objections left during review

The review did not dispute the observation that the failure exits were different, but it raised a more practical question: without confirming the current callers, was splitting out the entry actually isolating the problem, or was it merely renaming unknown caller relationships? That question was not answered in the first version.

Another objection concerned rollback cost. Restoring only the old entry seemed straightforward, but once someone had begun entering through the new entry, the old entry was no longer the only integration point. Conversely, keeping both sides for too long would make it impossible for callers to tell which one was the intended path. The old draft did not resolve this dilemma; it only left "whether rollback should restore only the old entry" as an unresolved item.

Someone also requested a contrasting input. The reason was not to pad the test count, but to avoid treating a phenomenon during a window transition as a path difference. The original plan was to use the damage state for this check, but no verifiable caller location was added. Therefore, there was no reason to advance the candidate route into a formal plan.

## Traces in later cards

After this proposal was written, related work was later tracked under MTRA-006 and MTRA-013, respectively. They are not approval records for this proposal; they are included here because, when reviewing the old route, people often follow these two numbers back.

MTRA-006 retains the routing for the old exit action: the card requires removing the action that points to the old exit action while retaining a snapshot of the route before the change. Subsequent records show that the item underwent risk review and, after entering processing, left a reminder: the expiration action lines up, but the current result in the card is still the old result. This reminder cannot be used to infer that splitting the entry had succeeded back then; it only indicates that, when later looking back at the old routing through the card, "current result" cannot be taken directly as the new result.

MTRA-013 concerns checking a dual-state client-client-integration object, requiring two states to be recorded in order of occurrence and first confirming whether they are the same object. It later entered processing. This action is similar to the concern in the old proposal: before the object relationship is confirmed, the two states can easily be mistaken for two call paths, or conversely, one path can be split into two objects. Card processing did not substitute for the caller verification that was missing at the time.

Therefore, these two cards are treated here as later review entry points, rather than being folded into the trial results of the original proposal. They also do not answer which caller path the damage state passed through, so they cannot be used to fill the blank intentionally left in the first version.

## Why This Route Was Not Adopted

Not adopting it does not mean that `compatibility entry` necessarily should not exist. Its value at the time was to separate and inspect the failure exits that had been mixed together; its shortcoming was that it first required knowing which callers would be affected by the new entry boundary. The material supports only the former judgment and is insufficient to support the conclusion that the latter assessment has been completed.

Continuing with `offline loading` was also not formally declared preferable. It merely avoided adding an integration fork while the object relationships had not yet been clarified. The old route is kept here to remind later readers: at the time, this was not a simple replacement of "old and new," but the abandonment, in the absence of a picture of the callers, of a trial method that might have been easier to observe but whose rollback conditions were also more ambiguous.

If this direction is reopened, the first things to fill in are not a complete migration plan but two concrete questions: exactly which entry the streaming-window phenomenon occurs after; and whether the damage state really still passes through the current caller. Only when there is verifiable material for both points is it worth revisiting whether to split out the compatibility entry separately or continue to leave the issue in the offline-loading path.

# Performance Lab Failed Run On-Call Guide

This page starts with a failed run. When a message comes in, first save the original input, the run ID (if available from the incident), the version used, and the first visible result. Screenshots can be attached, but don't leave only a screenshot; also write down the names that can take someone back to the file or run record in the handoff.

## Pin down the state first

Find the entry point used for this run from `docs/adj-shared/runbooks/Shared-performance-lab-failed-run-on-call-page.md`. Earlier pages treated `compatibility entry` as the starting point for every issue. That can still serve as the on-call starting point, but don't infer from it that all subsequent steps have been validated.

Don't restart, refresh permissions, or recreate data just because the page is blank. Only do those things when the actions themselves are conditions of this check. First preserve the original input, version, first error or empty result, and circle the first point of difference. Change only one condition in a comparison; if you replace data, clear the cache, and change the entry at the same time, you won't know which step caused the change.

If the version or input record from before the entry point is missing, stop here. Don't fill the blank with a default, and don't let a green result from a rerun overwrite the original state.

## First point of difference

- The entry opens, but no subsequent result appears: record the entry name and the object where it stopped; don't continue clicking through to the later `Lua binding`. Earlier versions wrote "`Lua binding` did not appear" as the stop condition; keep this as a historical observation. It has no accompanying recovery experiment, so it still only means stop; it cannot be interpreted as the root cause.
- The run reaches `vehicle model`, and only then does a difference appear: save that object's version and the previous normal sample. Don't just write "model failed"; write whether the first difference occurred during loading, replacement, or waiting for the next segment. If these states have no intermediate record, leave the empty window blank.
- There is no evidence of collection or execution: first check that the switch is actually enabled. If there is no evidence, don't fill in zero. The local check left by MTRB-004 makes the same point; it can only help locate the issue and cannot replace the original run artifact.
- When you need to inspect `streaming window` or the `WebP header`, treat it first as a checkpoint in the incident; do not treat the name as a success signal. If the checkpoint has no corresponding input and version, stop there.

## Old cold-cache case

A run associated with MTRB-001 first pinned the toolchain; the recorded action was `toolchain_pinned`. The current result appeared only after a cold cache; this shows that the cache state changed the observation, not that the expiry action has changed. The public addendum on the card still says: the expiry action is still the original result.

Later, the cold-cache result was attached separately to the card, while the original expiry action remained in place. When the test machine was occupied by another regression, this work once entered blocked status; that attempt produced no usable recovery conclusion. Before the test machine is available, don't rewrite "a result appeared after cold cache" as a stable reproduction, and don't delete the original failure record.

Therefore, when the same symptom occurs, keep two separate records: the first result of the original run and the result after the cold cache. Note the version used in both; change only the cache condition. If the entry, data, or permissions also changed between the two, stop the comparison and fill in the differences first.

## Stop, roll back, and hand off

When the first failure is clear but the recovery action has not been tried in the shared environment, stop at the failed step. Preserve the original input, version, error output, and the unrecorded time window. Keep the return action from the old page in the record, but it is not a validated rollback command; without evidence from the incident, do not execute an action reconstructed from memory.

You can go back to the most recent normal sample for a single-condition comparison. If the comparison still shows two differences, or the shared environment is occupied by another regression, stop and hand the run to the entry-point maintainer; don't rerun just to fill the window. Restoring the service does not mean the cause has been confirmed.

At minimum, write these incident fields in the handoff:

- Which entry was used and the object where it actually stopped;
- The original input, version, and first result;
- Whether a cold-cache run was done, and whether the cold-cache result was saved separately;
- Which condition was changed and which condition was left untouched;
- Whether `streaming window` has a record; if not, explicitly leave it blank;
- Whether the expiry action is still the original action, and whether the original owner was contacted.

The old arrangement under MTRB-002 was: contact the original owner before expiry; if there is no reply, close out under the existing expiry action. In the handoff, retain this historical arrangement and the contact outcome; don't record no reply as confirmed. MTRB-003 also require aligning shared-performance-lab with the current entry and leaving any window without a record blank.

On the next shift, use the same page entry point for the check, but first review the original artifacts and the first point of difference left in this handoff. If the page still does not match the incident state, stop at the object currently visible and record the difference separately; don't overwrite this failed run with the new result. DOC-37 records a comparison that changes only the current revision; switch to it only when actually performing that comparison.

# Migration Guide for the Compatibility Directory Entry Point

This page is still kept under the old approach: record the entry points first instead of announcing that the old path is gone. It covers the public contract formed around `CLuaCompatibilityDefs.cpp`, `CLuaCompatibilityDefs.h`, and the migration records that depend on it. The actual index is located at `docs/adj-server/migration/current-entry-old-entry-migration-index.md`. Even same-named directory entries that look similar should be logged separately first.

Earlier, the simplified assumption was: once the directory shows the current entry point, the old entry point can be marked as migrated. That assumption came from seeing only the category names at the time, without confirming all consumers. It was not removed from the page because many older records still use that wording; this round of work no longer treats it as a basis for retirement.

## What to Keep Beside the Old Path

Beside the old entry point, retain the original name and any alternative location that can be found. Beside the current entry point, record the object corresponding to `CLuaCompatibilityDefs.cpp` or `CLuaCompatibilityDefs.h`; if the two sides do not match, do not invent a new name that merely sounds plausible. In the consumer column, record only calls that explicitly identify the entry point; `offline loading` remains blank.

```text
old entry point ──────> current entry point ──────> confirmed callers
  │                  │
  └──── return to old entry point on rollback ────────┘
```

The arrows in the diagram show the order for tracing back, not proof that the switch is complete. One consumer being able to work through the current entry point does not mean that another consumer with the same name has completed migration. Continue tracking the old path, new path, and compatibility callers separately; do not write a blanket "compatible" entry at the end of the batch.

During a trial, keep the same consumer, input, and version fixed, and change only the entry point. Record the original input, the first visible result, and the status of the second call. A cleaned-up screenshot cannot replace the original record, because it cannot show whether the input, version, and failure location were all changed together. A result returned by the current entry point is not enough either; if the status of the second call differs from that of the old entry point, the batch remains pending confirmation.

## Two Later Addenda

In 2, a timing discrepancy in Server · Compatibility Catalog first appeared at the beginning of the month: the version timestamp in the old record and the object used later were not clearly written side by side. It was later also found that the execution record still pointed to the old repository or old source. The index therefore retains two pieces of information—the version and the source; do not directly substitute the new path for the old path's name. Keep `MTRC-002` as the navigation reference for this timing discrepancy.

Another record requires saving the minimal input, version, and rollback action before the retirement action becomes ineffective. It did not become a project-wide operational requirement; it applies only to this migration index: when the entry cannot be traced back from the location of `CLuaCompatibilityDefs.cpp` or `CLuaCompatibilityDefs.h`, return to the old entry point first and preserve the state. The corresponding entry point is `MTRC-005`.

Replaying adjacent inputs can help compare entry points, but cannot replace the caller list in the index. A single replay changes only one adjacent `server-compatibility-catalog`; all other conditions for the current entry point remain unchanged. It shows a comparison result, not confirmation from all adopters. `MTRC-003` recorded a case in which the last adopter confirmed only the shift record and did not confirm the current version, so it cannot be used to close the old path.

## Provisional Retirement Wording

Each migration batch must retain at least these four items: the old entry point, the current entry point, the consumer, and the version. If the version is missing, split same-named objects into two rows; if the consumer has not confirmed, do not rewrite it as completed in the notes. If any one of the entry point, code location, or original input does not match, restore the old entry point first, then review it once more with the original input.

The old entry point remains a rollback point; that does not mean it will be kept permanently. This wording replaces the old guidance that "maintaining the old path means leaving the old entry point untouched," but the old guidance remains in the historical section. The appearance of an alternative location in the directory, a schedule drawing near, or confirmation from a single consumer is not enough on its own to retire the old entry point.

versions.body:
# Compatibility Directory Entry Point Migration Notes

This index was not compiled in one pass as a cutover table. Initially, only classification differences were noted beside the filenames for the "current entry point"; only later did someone separate out the old entry points, replacement locations, code locations, and caller confirmations. As a result, the page mixes several approaches: some paragraphs treat directory names as indicators of progress, some require retaining the original input, and others put the version and adopter on the same line. The old paragraphs have not been cleaned up and still mislead people who read only the headings.

The index has always been located at `docs/adj-server/migration/current-entry-old-entry-migration-index.md`. It focuses on the public contracts built around `CLuaCompatibilityDefs.cpp` and `CLuaCompatibilityDefs.h`, migration records, and caller compatibility; this work has its own schedule, maintainers, and exit criteria. The page lists only old entry points, replacement locations, and callers still using them. Notes that cannot be traced back remain outdated.

## Older Statements in the Page Margins

The earliest classification approach wavered between two directions: continuing with `Damage Status`, or splitting out `Lua Bindings` separately. The reason for supporting the latter at the time was narrow: two sections of records in the index had different failure exits. At that point, the current callers of `Offline Loading` had not been confirmed, nor had it been decided whether a rollback would restore only the old entry point.

The wording at the time also included a simplified judgment: if the current entry point appeared in the directory, the migration was complete. This judgment was once used to reduce old directory entries, but it later became clear that it only showed that a name had been added to the index, not that compatible callers had switched over. It is retained here so that the old batch markers remain understandable; it is no longer a suitable basis for retiring the old entry point.

Another older statement was that "maintaining the old path" meant keeping the old entry point indefinitely. Later practice narrowed this to: until the caller and version have been confirmed, the old entry point must remain available as a rollback location that can be revisited. Both interpretations coexist, and the former is outdated. Do not retroactively rewrite the former as the latter, or it will become impossible to explain why the migration was not stopped earlier.

Some people initially also wanted to merge adjacent directory entries by name. That approach was not continued either. When `server-compatibility-catalog` entries share a name but lack version identifiers, they cannot be treated as the same object based on the short name alone; old and current entry points should not be joined into one record merely because their names are similar.

## The Four Fields in the Index

The index usually starts from the old entry point, rather than working backward from code files. The old entry point column stores the old name; the current entry point column stores the known replacement location; the caller column records only consumers whose entry points can already be identified; the version column records the object version corresponding to that row. If any field is missing, the entire row can still be kept, but it cannot be marked complete.

`CLuaCompatibilityDefs.cpp` and `CLuaCompatibilityDefs.h` are code locations for the public contracts, not an automatically generated list of callers. The index can mark an object as known only when the old entry point, current entry point, and actual consumer can be linked together. If only the directory name or only one of the files is visible, retain the name and the gap, rather than filling it in with an object from an adjacent project.

```text
Original input / old version ───────┐
                       ├─ Old entry point ──> Current entry point ──> Confirmed compatible callers
Rollback action ──────────────┘      │              │
                              └──────<───────┘
```

The return line in the diagram represents returning to the old entry point to reuse the original input after a failed migration, not that all callers can switch unconditionally in both directions. Nor does it mean that the current entry point has fully replaced the old one. Without a cross-reference for the code location, version, or consumer, the diagram can only help establish the order of the records, not fill in the missing original context.

Earlier versions treated `Damage Status` as the main entry point for the related calls. It was later confirmed only that its failure exit differed from that of the other section, not that it covered all compatible calls. Splitting out `Lua Bindings` was still just the migration classification used at the time; the index should no longer present this classification choice as a fact that holds for all callers.

## Changes in Recordkeeping

The timing discrepancy first emerged between the old records and later objects. An early-month check in 2 found that the version timestamp for Server · Compatibility Catalog had not been clearly recorded, and subsequent execution records still pointed to the old repository or the old source. If an old page said only "migrated", there was no way to tell which version or location it referred to, so later rows retain the version and source beside the entry point name. `MTRC-002` is the entry point for reviewing this timing discrepancy.

These added notes did not fix all the old rows. Same-named objects whose version identifiers have already been lost can still only be retained side by side; do not group them under a single current version just to make the table look tidy. `MTRC-009` documented this kind of gap. It shows that two same-named entries in the index may simply lack distinguishing information, not that either one has migrated.

Recording exit actions brought another change: before an action becomes invalid, the minimal input, version, and rollback action must be retained. The minimal input here means the original input used at the time to reproduce the entry point, not a sample prepared later. The first visible result must also be stored with the original input, or after replaying it there is no way to determine whether the change came from the entry point or the input. `MTRC-005` can be used to review this recordkeeping requirement.

Earlier, some people compared only cleaned-up screenshots and thought work could proceed as long as the current entry point returned a green result. This approach no longer applies. Screenshots cannot show the state of the second call or whether the version has already changed. A migration trial should retain the first visible result and the state of the second call; if they differ, do not mark the current entry point as compatible.

Input replay for the adjacent `server-compatibility-catalog` was added later solely to isolate differences between entry points: keep the consumer, input, and version fixed, and swap in only one adjacent directory object. It cannot replace confirmation from actual callers. The last adopter in `MTRC-003` confirmed only the records from that shift, not the current version, which is precisely an example of why replay results cannot be used to close the case directly.

## Batch Records and Actual Migration

Each batch moves only one consumer that can already be identified. First keep the old entry point readable, leave the original input and version unchanged, and change only the entry point. If the failure location changes, first record the failure location along with the input and version under that batch, then decide whether to roll back. Do not combine results from multiple consumers into a single "compatible" conclusion, and do not treat one directory update as multiple callers having switched over.

Batch rows can be filled in in the following order: first enter the old and current entry points; after confirming that they can be traced back to the objects in the index, fill in the consumer and version; only then record the observed results. When the version is blank, put the two same-named objects on separate rows; when the consumer is blank, retain the empty field. Such blanks are more useful than an incorrect completion marker, because it will still be possible later to tell whether the missing piece was the version or the caller.

The "replacement location" in old records is sometimes only a name that appears in the directory. Unless it can be traced back together with the corresponding object in `CLuaCompatibilityDefs.cpp` or `CLuaCompatibilityDefs.h`, and an actual consumer, it is still only a candidate location. Do not invent a new calling relationship for a candidate location, or delete the old entry point just because the candidate looks like the current entry point.

`MTRC-012` requires older judgments to be labeled with their time context, and then the new Server · Compatibility Catalog results to be appended alongside them. This page therefore allows two adjacent paragraphs to give different conclusions: an earlier paragraph may treat a directory update as completion, while a newer one requires both the consumer and version to match. They are kept side by side not because a contradiction has been left unresolved, but because the older criteria still have navigational value.

## Where to Return on Failure

First check whether the entry point actually points to the object registered in the index. Once the entry point matches, check whether the code location corresponds to `CLuaCompatibilityDefs.cpp` or `CLuaCompatibilityDefs.h`, and finally verify whether the original input and version have been replaced. If any of these three does not match, do not expand the migration scope; return to the old entry point, run through it again with the original input, and keep the discrepancy confined to that batch.

A result from the current entry point is not enough either. If the state of the second call differs from that of the old entry point, first record the location of the difference and the original result, and leave the status undetermined. Here, "restoring the old entry point" is only a rollback action, not deletion of the current entry point, much less a declaration that the split plan has been rejected. The current entry point can remain in the index and be revisited once the gaps in input, version, or caller information have been filled.

Access failure at the regular entry point is another boundary. When a non-administrator is denied access, the denial location and request/run id should be retained on the original card; this index does not turn it into a successful migration path. `MTRC-006` serves only to navigate back to that failure context. It cannot prove that the migration of `CLuaCompatibilityDefs.cpp` is complete, nor that the restricted details page and the regular entry point are part of the same issue.

When the original context is missing, do not recreate a sample that looks clean. The gap retained in `MTRC-015` is where the `server-compatibility-catalog` from that time, the current entry point, and the first visible current revision should be linked back to the index. This gap did not disappear automatically just because migration notes were added later; the old rows remain unverifiable.

## Retirement Markers for Old Entry Points

The label "can be retired" is now written beside a batch only when all three conditions align: the current entry point points to a specific version, the actual consumer confirms it can run through that entry point, and historical queries can still find the old entry point and the rollback action. If any one is missing, keep the old path. Reaching the scheduled date, having a replacement location in the directory, or receiving confirmation from one consumer cannot, on its own, substitute for these three conditions.

This paragraph is a narrower set of criteria added later and should not be backfilled into the earliest classification records. The original page had neither a version column nor all callers; therefore many "migrated" labels in old batches can only be understood as meaning that a current entry point had been found at the time, not that the old entry point can be retired today.

The maintainers and exit criteria for Server · Compatibility Catalog are determined by that project's own arrangements. The main project's status does not automatically carry over to the migration status here. The index still starts at `docs/adj-server/migration/current-entry-old-entry-migration-index.md`; text that cannot be traced back from there remains marked as old notes, and must not be overwritten with new filenames.

## Old Examples Not Yet Moved Out

- Old example: treating `Damage Status` as the unified entry point for all related calls. It was later confirmed only that its failure exit differed from that of the other section, which is not enough to account for splitting out `Lua Bindings`.

  │                         │

# Quality Signal Dashboard Entry Point Migration Guide

Migrating the entry points for utils-quality-signal is not simply a matter of replacing directory links. The index retains old entry points, current entry points, replacement locations, and callers still using them so that failure samples, regression layering, and the attribution of instability signals can still be traced back to the entry point in use at the time. The scope here centers on the failure samples produced by `test_build_gettext_catalog.py` and `test_build_gettext_catalog_nsi.py`, and the migration batches arranged around those samples.

The index file is still at `docs/adj-utils/migration/current-entry-old-entry-migration-index.md`. After opening the file, read each entry's source and adopters before deciding whether to change its link. Merging entries solely because they have the same name will conflate entry points from different revisions into one entry, making it impossible to tell which callers have already migrated away or which failure samples belong to the old path.

## What Each Index Row Should Retain

Give each old entry point its own row; do not treat the "old path" as a master switch. Add information to each row in the following order:

| Field | How to fill it in |
| --- | --- |
| Old entry point | Retain the original name and location; do not overwrite them with the current entry point |
| Current entry point | Enter the replacement location; if unconfirmed, mark it as pending verification rather than guessing the destination |
| Adopters | Register only callers still using it; keep separate rows for sources with the same name |
| revision | State the revision corresponding to this row to avoid mixing old and new displays |
| Sample | Point to the first observed failure sample and identify its regression layer |
| Retirement status | Trialed, rollback available, awaiting handoff, or cannot be taken offline |

Some original entries contain only a link and the statement "migrated." For these rows, add the adopters and retirement status first rather than rushing to change the link. If the current entry point exists but its adopters are unknown, that means the replacement location can be looked up, not that the old entry point can be deleted. Conversely, a caller having tried the current entry point does not justify erasing the old entry point's failure records.

Entry points with the same name must be separated by source. MTRD-015 records that two current entry points with the same name each need their own source and adopters retained; the index therefore does not use the shorthand "same name means same object." If only the name can be confirmed, but not the source, retain two rows pending verification. This may look redundant, but it is easier to recover from than mistakenly attributing an old entry point still in use to another one.

## Migration Starts with One Adopter

Each migration batch handles only one confirmed caller. Before starting, record the entry point it uses, the original input, the runtime environment, and the first observed result; then switch that caller to the current entry point and keep the old entry point readable or restorable. Write the replacement location for the current entry point back to the index; do not record temporary trial results as a full migration.

```text
Old entry point record ── Original input and failure sample ──> Retain
      │
      ├── One confirmed adopter ──> Current entry point record
      │                              │
      │                              ├── Matching results: retain trial record
      │                              └── Different results: restore old entry point mapping
      │
      └── Other adopters ──> Leave for the next batch, unchanged by this batch
```

The second check after the trial still uses the original input. Compare the results, error patterns, and state after another invocation, not screenshots compiled afterward. Regression layering is meaningful only when comparable records for both the current and old entry points are retained in the entry. Without the original input, you can record that "a failure was observed," but cannot use it to judge whether the migration succeeded.

Archive the failure samples for `test_build_gettext_catalog.py` and `test_build_gettext_catalog_nsi.py` separately. When both fail, first record which regression layer each falls into; when only one side fails, first treat it as an entry-point-related instability signal rather than immediately attributing the cause to the entire build pipeline. Even if a sample turns green after a rerun, retain the record of the first failure and the environment used so that the index does not contain only the final state.

Instability signals need their own attribution column. Record the samples observed, their regression layers, and whether they reproduce with the same input; mark entries without reproduction evidence only as undetermined. Migration batches must not use "unstable" in place of a retirement decision: whether the old entry point can be removed, whether the current entry point has been adopted, and whether the failure samples are comparable remain three separate questions.

## Retirement Actions and Revisions to Earlier Records

The earlier practice treated the appearance of the current entry point in the directory as a sign of near completion. This practice is no longer used. After MTRD-011, the index requires the two utils-quality-signal entries to be separated by revision, and old links must not be overwritten with new links; MTRD-014 further requires events, utils-quality-signal, and index timestamps to be aligned, with unexplained time differences retained separately. The index's chronological order is therefore determined not by the page's last modification, but by the events and revision corresponding to each entry.

The old routing issue in MTRD-003 also affects retirement decisions: execution records had been sent to a receiving team that was no longer active. Before migrating, first confirm where records for the current entry point are received; changing only the caller without changing this routing layer will make the current entry point appear usable while leaving no actionable records when failures occur. Retain a written explanation of the old routing until it has been fully verified; it must not be replaced with a blank.

MTRD-007 documented another incomplete state: the person handing it over had already entered a timestamp, but the person taking over the entry point being retired had not signed. Mark such entries as "awaiting handoff" and continue retaining the old entry point. During testing, the handoff must go to someone who can modify the fixtures, and the maintainer should also be listed based on this actual ability to handle the work; if that field is empty, leave it empty rather than filling it with a historical team name.

After the toolchain was pinned in MTRD-004, failure samples and rollback checks should both continue using the same environment. This item was blocked at one point because the test machine was occupied by other regression runs, so batches without rerun records cannot be marked as passed. The index may note that the machine is occupied and samples are pending addition, but must not count a waiting state as migration completion.

## When to Roll Back

If any of the following occurs, first stop expanding the batch: the current and old entry points produce different results for the same input; the error pattern changes without samples to explain it; the state differs on the second invocation; the handoff destination for the current entry point is unconfirmed; or the entry point being retired still has no one to take it over. Stopping expansion does not mean deleting the current entry point's entry; the index retains the trial location and observed behavior so that the next check can continue from the same place.

When rolling back, first restore the old entry point mapping used by that caller, then confirm that the old entry point can receive the original input. Next, use the pinned toolchain to review the layer containing the sample from the first failure. Retain the current entry point's entry, trial records, and failure samples; rollback changes the adoption relationship rather than erasing the trial that already took place. If the old entry point can be restored and the current entry point remains queryable, the next batch can restart once the handoff information has been completed.

Entries lacking a rollback command or explicit stop conditions must not be added to the decommissioning list. The gaps in retirement actions noted in MTRD-004 still apply: first write the restoration target and stopping point in the index row, then discuss whether to shut down the old entry point. If a caller has confirmed only the replacement location, but not the restoration method, the status remains available for trial, not retired.

## Index Maintenance Cadence

Index updates follow migration batches rather than overwriting the entire page with one round of results all at once. An update usually changes only the row for one caller, its revision, sample location, and retirement status. Even neighboring entries with similar names must wait until their respective sources and adopters are confirmed. This preserves separate records for old entry points, new entry points, and compatible callers, preventing a later batch's results from rewriting the circumstances of an earlier batch.

Explanations that cannot be checked against their sources remain marked as outdated. They still tell readers that there was once an entry point or adoption relationship to verify, but are no longer treated as current conclusions. Once a verifiable source is found, add it to the original row; if it is confirmed to belong to another entry point with the same name, add a corresponding row rather than silently changing the old explanation to the new source.

MTRD-003, MTRD-004, MTRD-007, MTRD-011, MTRD-014, and MTRD-015 record issues with routing, retirement, handoff, mixed displays, reversed chronology, and same-name sources, respectively. When you encounter the first broken link, refer to the field notes at DOC-43; only entry point migration, failure samples, and retirement status are maintained here, and broken-link observations are not folded into migration conclusions.

A row can be changed from trial to complete only when it has a confirmed adopter, the current entry point location, comparable failure samples or regression records, and an executable restoration procedure. All other rows remain in the index for continued maintenance.

# Protocol Enum Freeze: Entry-Point Code Walkthrough

Anyone taking this over should start with the public entry point for multiplayer-runtime. Don't start by searching for a batch of same-named files using "protocol" or "enum". You can currently use `Client/sdk/multiplayer/CMultiplayer.h` as a starting point; it directs the search toward the multiplayer interfaces, but does not explain ownership of the protocol enum freeze itself.

Tentative route:

```text
multiplayer-runtime
  -> CMultiplayer.h
  -> a direct caller
  -> the first actual consumer of the protocol enum freeze
```

The offline dependency list can help narrow down the next hop, but an object with the same name appearing in the list does not mean a call edge exists. Start by following one direct caller; stop at the first place that actually consumes the protocol enum freeze. If you then need to determine who maintains the freeze or whether there are other consumer branches, another owner needs to answer; the initial draft won't fill that in with guesses.

versions.body:
# Protocol Enum Freeze: Entry-Point Code Tour

At the initial handover, the search results mixed interface files, entries in the dependency list, and several objects with the same name. All of them suggested a connection to the protocol enum freeze, but none answered which layer contained the actual entry point. After review, `Client/sdk/multiplayer/CMultiplayer.h` was retained as the starting point: it is useful for confirming that the search enters from the multiplayer side, but not for establishing ownership of protocol enum maintenance.

This trace covers just one thing: select one direct caller from this starting point, then continue to the first actual consumer of the protocol enum freeze. Do not expand into every protocol use in the first file, or treat adjacent entries in the dependency list as part of the call chain. This keeps the path short, but lets the person taking over retrace it.

```text
multiplayer-runtime public entry point
        |
        v
Client/sdk/multiplayer/CMultiplayer.h
        |
        v
One direct caller
        |
        v
First actual consumer of the protocol enum freeze
```

## Using the starting point

When starting from `CMultiplayer.h`, first write down that the target being traced is the "entry point for the protocol enum freeze," not "all multiplayer code." This prevents later searches from being led astray by implementations or documentation with similar names. The file path serves as a locator here: it identifies the area containing the Multiplayer Runtime interface and lets the next step narrow the search around actual call relationships.

For the first step, find only one direct caller. Once selected, follow that caller's actual usage rather than keeping multiple candidate branches open at once. If a candidate appears only in a comment, list, or filename, keep it as a signpost for the time being; it has no call edge and cannot stand in for this hop. This is exactly where mistakes were easy to make before: treating "same name" as "already connected" makes the route unreliable from the start.

## Offline dependency list

The offline dependency list is still useful, but its role is narrow. It can help identify objects worth revisiting and let the person taking over know that a name was once included in the dependency scope. The list alone cannot establish call order, much less identify who consumes the protocol enum freeze.

In practice, treat the list as a catalog of candidates:

- First, anchor the entry point at `CMultiplayer.h`;
- Use the list to narrow down potentially relevant call sites;
- Return to direct call relationships and select one edge to follow;
- Stop expanding once you reach the first actual consumer.

Here, "actual consumer" means the first point in the call path that actually needs the protocol enum freeze, not an object whose name contains "protocol" or "enum." If a file with the same name has no such call relationship, just retain its location; do not describe it as an entry point on this page.

## Recording the reviewed path

During review, stop piling up results by filename. Instead, leave a brief note for each node visited. For each hop, record only three things: where it came from, why the trace can continue to the next point, and whether the first consumer has already been reached here. This keeps the offline list, interface path, and call edges in their proper roles.

For example, the note for `CMultiplayer.h` should identify it as the starting point; the note for the direct caller should explain how it connects to the previous hop; and the note for the first consumer should state that the trace ends there. There is no need to add every subsequent use site. The scope of propagation after the protocol enum freeze is a separate question. Adding it to this entry-point route would obscure the edge the trace was meant to find.

The review also confirmed a handling rule: objects with the same name can help locate things again, but they cannot be used to skip the direct caller. When a file has the same name but no call edge, do not delete it yet or record it as evidence of failure; it is just a signpost for a later search. Keeping it that way is better than mixing it into the main route.

## Stop at the handover boundary

This page ends when the first actual consumer is reached. The next questions may concern maintenance constraints on the enum freeze, whether other consumers share the same semantics, or who confirms changes to the freeze. Those questions require answers from another owner; this record does not include them in the established path.

When taking over, first retrace the diagram, then add any newly discovered direct call edges to the corresponding nodes. If you can find only objects with the same name but no call relationship, return to `CMultiplayer.h` and the selected direct caller rather than continuing to widen the search. This at least distinguishes "the edge has not been found yet" from "the trace has reached maintenance questions beyond the consumer."
