versions.body:
# Vehicle Lifecycle Integration Test Deviation Postmortem

During the vehicle lifecycle integration test window, the visible results did not appear as originally planned. The final state did not remain failed throughout: there was a temporary recovery before the window ended, making the initial deviation look like a brief fluctuation. For integration testing, the sequence observed during the window therefore could not establish stability, and seeing recovery at the end could not prove that the original plan had held continuously.

This record preserves the sequence observed on shift, not a complete causal account reconstructed afterward. The investigation notes used `Client/sdk/game/CFxManager.h` and the call name used at the time to trace back; that location helped align what was being observed, but was not treated as the permanent home of the vehicle lifecycle.

## Window Records

- The first observation when checking vehicle lifecycle results against the original plan was a mismatch between the visible results and the plan.
- Attention initially went to the end of the window because a temporary recovery had followed the deviation; the on-site evidence was insufficient to link that recovery to any particular state change.
- The investigation retained records of the public calls, along with an adjacent counterexample: the counterexample did not show the same visible deviation, but this was not enough to establish that the two paths differed in only one respect.
- QA review did not accept "recovered at the end" as grounds for a pass, and added an observation checkpoint: record the first visible divergence in state transitions; do not let final success obscure intermediate states.

## Explanation at the Time

The initial on-call assessment was that, since the expected results were visible again at the end of the window, this could be treated as a return to alignment with the plan. That assessment described only what was seen after recovery. It did not explain when the deviation began or whether the temporary recovery covered the same stretch of state transitions. It is retained because the on-call staff did continue integration testing on that basis; the checkpoint added later should not be retroactively written in as a cause already understood at the time.

The temporary recovery should only be taken to mean what it did at the time: it allowed the window to close, but did not establish a root cause. The public calls and the adjacent counterexample only indicated a need to narrow observations to the area around the first divergence; they did not establish the caller, the vehicle object, or the lifecycle stage as the source of the problem.

## Still Unresolved

The on-site records are insufficient to determine whether there were repeated transitions involving the same state around the first visible divergence. There is also no conclusion on why the adjacent counterexample was unaffected. Future references to this deviation should include both the intermediate-state records and the recovery records from the end of the window; retaining only the final success will lead back to the same overly optimistic assessment made at the time.

title: Client Offline Rerun FAQ

# Client Offline Rerun FAQ

During offline rerun week, the most common questions weren't about rerun commands, but whether the existing performance-runtime entry point actually counted as confirmation, who would withdraw a candidate path when no one was pursuing it, and what state counted as closure.

**What can the existing entry point prove?**

The earlier position was: as long as the entry point was still there, the candidate path could be treated as ready to rerun. That judgment was only meant to let work on the ground continue; the entry point itself did not indicate whether the samples covered adjacent boundaries.

**Who withdraws the candidate path?**

No specific name was recorded here. When some people continued using the entry point and others stopped a candidate path, closure and withdrawal were often written up as the same thing.

**When can it be closed?**

The provisional note is to revisit this after the samples finish running. We haven't yet determined whether there's a separate checklist for cross-platform enumeration.

# Client Offline Rerun FAQ

The review brought us back to the performance-runtime entry point. The old answer treated "the entry point opens" as "the candidate path has already been rerun." That overstated what it showed. The entry point only takes people back to the rerun location used at the time; it doesn't confirm cross-endpoint enums or check offline fallback on anyone's behalf.

**What can the entry point still be used for?**

Keep it as a lead for finding the candidate path again. If all that's left is an old link or screenshot, first confirm that the link still points to the same path, then decide whether to rerun. Don't substitute one successful attempt to open it for sample results.

**Who is responsible for withdrawal?**

There still isn't a clear answer. The second pass didn't find a separate withdrawal record, so "this path is no longer used" doesn't tell us who made the decision. When withdrawal is needed, the path and the closure status should at least be documented separately.

**What's still missing for closure?**

At the time, the additions only covered adjacent boundary samples. The original record didn't settle whether cross-endpoint enums, lifecycle, and the offline fallback entry point also had to be confirmed together. We can log the cross-endpoint enum checklist, but can't answer that here yet.

versions.body:
# Client Offline Rerun FAQ

These answers started as informal guidance passed around during offline rerun week. They were later used to explain whether candidate paths should be kept or dropped. The old text didn't distinguish "being able to find the entry point" from "having completed a rerun," and also conflated who withdraws the path with the conditions for closure. Traces of those old answers are retained below so the same misreading doesn't get treated as an agreement again.

**What does the performance-runtime entry point represent now?**

It's still the starting point for returning to the candidate path. The old answer said, "As long as the entry point is still there, we can keep moving toward closure." That line stays: people did proceed on that basis at the time. But the entry point's existence only means there's still somewhere to go back and check. It doesn't mean adjacent boundary samples have already been rerun by someone other than the implementer, nor that cross-endpoint enums and lifecycle haven't changed. Someone followed an old link and saw only the original candidates; that isn't grounds for marking the path as ready to close.

If the entry point won't open, don't automatically treat the candidate path as withdrawn. The old link may simply not have been tidied up. Conversely, the fact that the entry point still opens doesn't mean the candidate path should still be kept. What's retained here is the judgment used during rerun week, not the present-day rules for archiving candidate paths.

**Who actually withdraws a candidate path?**

There isn't a single reliable answer. The old version vaguely assigned this to "the person hooking up the entry point." The review couldn't establish whether that was the actual division of responsibilities or just a convenient shorthand used on site. So this page can't assign an owner to the withdrawal action. When a path is no longer used, first spell out "stop trying it" and "allowed to close" separately; neither can be inferred from the entry point's status alone.

**Under what conditions can it be closed?**

The team continues to use this rule: "The closeout card may only be closed once a non-implementer has completed a successful rerun using adjacent boundary samples and confirmed that the cross-endpoint enums, lifecycle, and offline fallback entry point remain valid." This restriction was added alongside the old guidance later, and explains why a single successful local offline run isn't enough.

"Non-implementer" isn't an additional approval role. It just means the person doing the rerun must not be the person who implemented this candidate path. Adjacent boundary samples aren't just any different client state, either; they're samples right at the candidate path's boundaries. Some people previously skipped over these two points and treated rerun week as an entry-point inspection.

This page still has no definite answer about the cross-endpoint enum checklist. The gap can be logged, but "no checklist yet" cannot be read as confirmation that the enums have been checked. For the single-variable record on protocol enums, see DOC-50; it doesn't supply a withdrawal owner for these three questions.
versions.change_summary: Corrected the old answer that conflated the entry point with closure

The team continues to use this rule: "The closeout card may only be closed once a non-implementer has completed a successful rerun using adjacent boundary samples and confirmed that the cross-endpoint enums, lifecycle, and offline fallback entry point remain valid." Questions about the missing cross-endpoint enum checklist can be logged, but the answer is explicitly left unknown.

versions.body:
# Protocol Enumeration Freeze: Single-Variable Trial Run Log

This review still lays out `streaming-runtime`'s repository state, call entry point, and offline dependency list side by side. Each of the three has its own place in the record: the repository state sets the scope of the code snapshot seen in this round, the call entry point is the starting point used for tracing back, and the offline dependency list preserves the specific list used in the comparison at that time. They are not three interchangeable candidates; this round did not look for a new entry point while rewriting the list.

The single-variable constraint remains in place. Each round changes only one input condition that has already been selected; the other two remain as they were in the first round. This arrangement is not meant to reduce subsequent states to some fixed conclusion, but to keep the first difference traceable to that change. If the entry point and list change at the same time, then even different migration states observed afterward cannot be compared as part of this set of records.

The first round's exact wording was "Protocol enumeration is not frozen yet." This wording describes the observed state when the state transition reached the first visible fork, not an attribution to the call entry point or offline dependencies. At the time, the record stopped at the fork: it did not record state transitions that might continue afterward as confirmed results, nor did it exclude either the call entry point or offline dependencies from the comparison scope. This stopping point remains useful because it preserves the location where the fork was first seen.

The review revisited the repository state, entry point, and list in the same order. The new record did not use the third run's result to overwrite the results from the first two rounds, nor use the final summary to replace the intermediate states left before and after the fork. The only thing the available material can confirm is that, under this fixed comparison, the state transition first diverged at that point. The record does not answer whether the paths rejoin in another state after the fork; extending "not frozen" into a judgment about the entire subsequent run would go beyond what this rerun actually recorded.

`Client/game_sa/CStreamingSA.h` continues to serve as the lookup point for finding streaming-related locations and call names. The first round traced back from here, and the review did not switch to another path to explain the fork. The filename and location make it easy to find that inspection context again, but they do not mean that protocol enumeration permanently belongs to this file, nor can this location alone draw a line of responsibility between the call entry point and the offline dependency list. The old notes call it the starting point; retaining that wording is more appropriate than adding a conclusion about ownership.

The order on this page was therefore not rearranged to reflect a final result: it first preserves the first visible fork, then notes which objects were unchanged during the review. If someone later sees only a seemingly successful state, they should still go back to the intermediate records from the first two rounds rather than work backward to revise the first round's judgment. The first round's observed state may be incomplete, but it should not be erased by a later end state.

The next rerun will again change only one selected input condition and record the new first fork alongside this round's record. If the rerun requires changing the call entry point, or if the offline dependency list is no longer the same list, start a separate record; do not combine the two types of change in the same comparison.
